maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED    REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF POSITION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED    REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited have given an undertaking, provided they receive the go-ahead from the government, to build a pipe line through Canada within five years, and also what is the present position of the propositions now before the government with reference to this matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED    REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been no developments since I answered a somewhat similar question a few days ago in the house. The company is endeavouring to get commitments from other interests which are required to create a situation which would facilitate the financing of its undertaking, and there have been no developments since I last mentioned the matter in the house.
With respect to the specific time limit that has been discussed with the company, it is probable that instead of there being an undertaking with a limit fixed in months or years it would be an undertaking that would mature when markets had developed to a certain percentage. It is felt that it would not be helpful to make any stipulation that would not be apt to be realized if the financial houses were not satisfied with the conditions that had developed with respect to the economic prospects of the undertaking. This is an undertaking the cost of which will run into hundreds of millions of dollars wdiich would have to be provided through financing by the public generally. We have to be realistic and recognize that it would not be useful to have an undertaking if the factual situation does not develop to make it an undertaking based on sound economics. I think the officers of the company are doing their best at this moment to get the kind of commitments that will make the prospects reasonably secure.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED    REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question? Has there been any change in the government policy announced in 1953 that the needs of the Canadian people for natural gas must be assured before there is any permission to export?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED    REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF POSITION
speechtext:
There has been no change in the general policy. Consideration is being given to the kind of situation that had to be met with respect to providing gas for Vancouver. There, there had to be a pipe line that will have a capacity greater than the quantity of gas Vancouver can consume at


this time, and so there has been an arrangement to allow the surplus that would be carried in the pipe line to be exported. Similar considerations may apply to a pipe line that would bring gas eastward. It may be that at this time it would have to have a greater capacity than the Canadian market in eastern Canada would now absorb. The question that is being discussed and about which negotiations are proceeding is to find what could be done with that surplus over and above eastern requirements at this time without making commitments that would not leave the gas available when the eastern Canadian market will have further developed.

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED    REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask just one other supplementary question, if I may. I cannot refer in detail to the article by Victor Mackie in the Free Press, but I ask the Prime Minister this. Did the government demand and receive a firm undertaking from the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines that, should it receive the approval of the government to proceed, that company would proceed within the five-year period? When may it be expected that a decision will be made on this question and, in particular, in reference to the alternative suggestions or offers that have been made?

maintopic: TRANS-CANADA PIPE LINES LIMITED    REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF POSITION
speechtext: I cannot fix any specific date. I am satisfied that they are proceeding just as expeditiously as they can to secure the commitments that would be required to make the proposal one that financial houses would look upon with favour. As I said a moment ago, it may be difficult to get a commitment that such and such will be done on such a date. We may have to be satisfied with a commitment that all efforts will be made to develop the market and that, when it reaches a certain quota, the commitment will then become an absolute obligation.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the discussion of the rules on July 1 was on a very high plane. I have just a few remarks to make about the proposals that are before us at the present time.

Eighteen years ago I was a member of the empire parliamentary conference. At a sitting of that conference, which took place at Westminster hall on May 6, 1937, the coronation year of the late King and the Queen Mother, I mentioned the rules of the house. Hon. members know that for centuries the British rules were few in number. The first one dates from 1707. It was standing order No. 63. Then there were two others, one in 1713, No. 6 and one in 1715, No. 65. The next one is 1821, No. 66. Therefore between 1707 and 1821 there were only four standing orders in force at Westminster and they referred to public money. In 1835 another standing order was passed, namely No. 81, to the effect that seats were not to be taken by members before prayers. In 1842 five standing orders were passed by the House of Commons, namely Nos. 75 to 79, relating to public petitions. Therefore at the time when May published the first edition of his valuable treatise only 10 standing orders were in force in the house at Westminster.
I thought that it might be of some interest to write a book on the rules of the various legislatures of the commonwealth. As one always does before writing a textbook, I made my own library. I obtained the rules up to date in 1937 from each legislature of the empire and I started my work on the standing orders of Australia. They were much more numerous than ours. I made my tabulations with great care in order to show what rules were the same in the larger number of the legislatures of the British Empire.
Then I went to Longmans, Green and Company in the shadow of St. Paul's cathedral and a reader gave me an interview. He was a very bright gentleman. He was a mind reader who could finish my sentences. It was an easy conversation. I showed him my notes or my tabulation and I asked him whether it was worth while writing a book on those lines. He said: Leave it with me and I will answer you in two or three days. When I returned to see him, he was friendly and he told me this: "Young man, if you want to write a book like this you may do so, but do not undertake such a work unless you have a foundation behind you because nobody will read it; nobody reads the rules."
What he said is true. I had proof of that fact when, after my speech, a gentleman by the name of Mr. F. W. Schramm, M.P. from New Zealand, said that he was delighted to have travelled 10,000 miles to listen to a great man like Sir John Simon; then he said: "What is the use of speaking of such a large number of rules when nobody pays any attention to them?" That was my experience. I destroyed my manuscript, which represented
12, 1955
Special Committee on Procedure some work, but it gave me the opportunity to realize what the rules of the house are.
The book of standing orders is divided into two parts. One part relates to the discussion of public bills and the other to the discussion of private bills. There should be another distinction made with respect to the duties of the clerk and assistant clerk of the house and the chief of orders because there are many rules that do not interest members. They are those that relate to the compilation of the orders of the day and Votes and Proceedings. When we come here we have two booklets in front of us. Votes and Proceedings relates to what has been done on the previous day and the orders of the day are the agenda for the present day. No member of the house, except possibly the leader of the house with the advice of the leaders of the other groups, has anything to do with them. It is done mostly by the chief of orders and notices and the clerk and assistant clerk of the house.
Therefore there are many rules that concern the members but which they are not interested in reading, and most of the time they take for granted that the work done by the officers of the house is satisfactory. In my personal knowledge extending over 31 years I do not recall a complaint being made by any member about the priority of one matter over another. Perhaps it has been suggested once or twice. Therefore, leaving aside those rules that concern the officers of the house gives us the opportunity to read the rules that are the shield and armour of members when they are engaged in debate or discussion. They are very few. Of course there are the rules of good education. One shall not be covered when he addresses the chair. We learned that in our families. It is nothing extraordinary.
There is a practice that members can wear their hats when they sit in the house. It came about because of the drafts at Westminster. They had to protect their skulls against the drafts coming across the hall. There is another practice that when members rise to speak during a division they must be covered. Not very long ago a member of parliament had to borrow a hat from a lady member to cover his head when he was addressing the chair during a division. But that is exceptional and it is rather ridiculous. It is outdated and out of fashion, and nobody would think of following tradition to that extent.
Now, what is the rule about sittings? Is it necessary to learn it by heart? I do not think so because the bells are there to summon the members. Sometimes they do not

Special Committee on Procedure ring long enough and we happen to arrive during the prayers. We miss the prayers because the ringing of the bells has been too short, but the bells are heard by all members of the house. Then there is another rule concerning the quorum, which is 20 members. If some members wish to object to what is said when there is a lack of a quorum they may do so. It happens very seldom, and the chair is always indulgent and waits until more members come to give a decision.
Then there is a rule to the effect that Mr. Speaker shall preserve order and decorum. There is standing order No. 15 concerning the business of the house and the orders of the day which are prepared by the chief of orders and notices and the clerks of the house.
Standing order No. 16 is a very important one and makes provision for the immediate consideration of any matter of privilege. This is fair because when there is an argument between two members, and a member objects to anything offensive which has been said, he may rise in the house. A member may exercise his right to rise on a question of privilege if any insults have been published in the press for speeches given outside of parliament. If some newspaper attacks a member of parliament, he has a right to defend himself and to defend his honour as a member of parliament in the very chamber where he is sitting. There is no question about it, because if the offensive language is used against the member in his capacity as a member of parliament, he has a right to defend himself in the House of Commons; that is clear.
Naturally, there is abuse of the privilege at times. There are some members who rise to say that their hockey team or rugby team has won something, and that is of no interest to the lawmakers of the country. It is very good publicity, and we must be tolerant in cases like that because they make members so happy in the thought that the best sportsmen in Canada live in their constituency and have accomplished a remarkable success.
To continue my line of argument, sir, standing orders Nos. 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25 and 26 refer to the clerk of the house. Then, standing order No. 37 concerns the limitation of speeches. I feel that 20 minutes is long enough for a speech, provided that one is not interrupted and provided that no sermon is made during the speech. Then, one can go on and express what he has to say in 20 minutes. This rule is not fair because there are exceptions for some cabinet members and some members of the opposition. I do not see why these gentlemen could not answer any charge in 20 minutes, except


when they have to reply to specific accusations and they have to read some papers which form part of the evidence.
Then, there is the rule concerning debatable motions, and there is a list of them. There are many members who rise to speak to motions, but it is for the Chair to decide whether or not a motion is debatable.
Standing order No. 40 says that members have a right to explain their point of view, and it refers also to irrelevance or repetition. I am never so happy as when one of my colleagues says the thing I would have liked to say before I speak. This is in accordance with the law of the least effort, and it is a great joy to hear what I wanted to say said by another member.
Under standing order No. 41 no member shall speak disrespectfully of Her Majesty, and offensive language against any member of parliament is forbidden. There is something that surprises me about this rule. It extends not only to Her Majesty but also to the governor or person administering the government of Canada. The order reads:
No member shall speak disrespectfully of Her Majesty, nor of any of the royal family: nor of the governor or person administering the government of Canada; nor use offensive words against either house, or against any member thereof.
If it applies to the royal family, it should apply also to the whole family of the governor general and the person administering the government of Canada in his absence. Nobody attacks them, but it would be fair to put them on the same standing as the royal family. The order continues:	\
No member may reflect upon any vote of the house, except for the purpose of moving that such vote be rescinded.
Standing order 41 goes with standing order 16, which reads:
Whenever any matter of privilege arises it shall be taken into consideration immediately.
We can ask a colleague to withdraw when he uses offensive language, but not when he has made an erroneous statement which contains nothing offensive. For instance, if a member says that a minister has not consulted his colleagues, it is a statement of fact. The minister rises and says: "I have consulted my colleagues." The matter is closed. If a member uses offensive language against any one of his colleagues, the member concerned may rise and ask for a withdrawal, but the member is bound to withdraw only offensive language, not a statement of fact which might be erroneous, but which contains nothing offensive in itself. Well, that is about all.
Questions are given to the clerk. A few years ago it was not necessary to sign them. Now they have decided the members should

sign the questions. If we give two copies of the questions it helps the officers of the house downstairs, and it is a very simple matter. The questions shall contain no statement of fact; that is all.
I have come to the conclusion that Mr. Schramm of New Zealand was right when he said that nobody paid any attention to the rules of the house and the discussion was nevertheless carried on satisfactorily. You remember, sir, that I complained not so long ago that a big concern like the Canadian National Railways had no regulation with respect to discussion. It is provided for in the new act that they are to have bylaws concerning the discussions at their meetings. That is new. I asked the Canadian Bankers Association whether they had any rules governing the annual meetings of the shareholders or the meetings of the board of directors and they said, "We never heard about it", but the discussion is carried on very well because, as the Minister of Finance, the leader of the house, mentioned the other day, it must always be carried on in a spirit of fairness.
One should not be too punctilious and too dogmatic about the rules. I remember that one of the predecessors of the present leader of the house referred at one time to rule 510, and I told him there was no such rule. Afterwards the word "citation" instead of the word "quotation" was used. What is that citation? That citation is a quotation from a ruling that may have been made 200 or 300 years ago, before the standing orders existed at Westminster, by a gentleman who happened to be Speaker, who made a decision under circumstances and conditions entirely different from those in which we live. Are we bound by that? What was the case before that Speaker? We do not know. That is why I said that most of the books which have been manufactured by Pepper, scissors and glue, the dicta of Redlich and all the other illustrious men, Anson, Bourinot, Sir Courtenay Ilbert and Beauchesne, were very easily manufactured. One had only to have the excerpts copied and then put them in disorder, in complete disorder. Cut them out with scissors and have them glued by Pepper, who was messenger to His Grace, and it was the rules of the house. Nobody understood anything in them, but there was one expert who could tell the government and the opposition, who wrote the rules of the house, and finally the books came out as an anthology of learning. I do not believe in it; I never did. I believe that the discussion should be according to the unwritten rules of fair discussion and debate, and then everybody would be satisfied. It would be in order; everybody would be satisfied. The less regard
Special Committee on Procedure we pay to the obsolete precedents the better we are, because these British precedents are completely ignored in Westminster at the present time. The Chair must have a broad outlook and be fair to members of parliament, as you are, sir, in order that they may fulfil their painstaking duties with the greatest ease and without any discrimination.
It is very easy for hon. members to understand the rules that concern them, because they are very few. They are clear enough to be understood by members who are not experts.
With regard to legislation, it is very seldom that members sponsor public bills, and when they do those bills do not go very far. I remember that I succeeded in having a bill passed in a few minutes to abolish one of the boards that had been created some years ago. I sponsored legislation to repeal the economic council act, and it was passed. It went out like that, but there was a barrage in the caucus the same day. I also sponsored bills to repeal the social legislation of the Conservative government which had been declared void by the privy council, but the prime minister of the time, Mr. Mackenzie King, adjourned the debate on each bill and it was never resumed.
The time is late and members have made concessions to each other in order to expedite the business of the house and I shall not insist upon this any further. What I want to say is that for 31 years in the House of Commons I have been more or less active. On looking up the index I find that I have made more speeches than any member of parliament. I have never bothered about the rules because I believed in the fairness of the Speakers when there was any difficulty.
I was glad that the prime minister and the government recognized the merits of Speaker Black and Speaker Bowman in appointing them members of the privy council. Other Speakers were appointed to the privy council upon leaving office but it took a Liberal government to give this deserved reward to these Conservative Speakers.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext: No one else could do it because there has been a Liberal government in office.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
It was done for others and it could have been done at the time, but they had so many other things to pack up that they did not have time to look after their friends. I think hon. gentlemen should give credit to the Liberal government for rewarding those two gentlemen who left many fond memories among those who knew them. My dealings with the members of the house have been most pleasant and I think one of

Special Committee on Procedure the finest rewards of a member of parliament in fulfilling his arduous duties is the many lasting friendships he makes among members on all sides of the house. I am known as a die-hard Liberal but I have many friends across the house and I shall remember them with emotion. I thank hon. members for having listened to these remarks on the rules.
Before concluding may I say what I have said to hon. members who have asked me to explain the rules to them. I said that it was easy to know the rules, it was easy to abide by the rules, provided the members are dealt with fairly in all circumstances.
Mr. Cold well: Mr. Chairman, we have just listened to a most interesting and characteristic speech by the hon. member for Temis-couata. He gave us the background of many of the rules of the House of Commons. I was most interested in his explanation of some of the old customs that have died out. When I first came to the house there were probably half a dozen members who used to insist on wearing their hats during the sittings, but I cannot recall any time in the last several years when an hon. member has followed that old custom. For example, 1 remember the Hon. Mr. Motherwell sitting in the chamber with his hat on, and I remember a former senator who used to represent a Quebec constituency in this house invariably wearing his hat in the chamber.
The historic background given this morning by the hon. member is rather different from what I learned when I was at school. I was told that the custom arose because in ancient times when the knights entered the House of Commons they wore their helmets in order to protect themselves should anything occur during a turmoil in the House of Commons. Similarly, in the house at Westminster the distance between the opposition and the government side of the house is exactly two swords' length, so that they cannot poke each other across the way. When I look at the mace I am reminded that it was once a club in the hands of the gentleman who occupied a position analogous to that of the Sergeant-at-Arms so that he could maintain order in the assembly.
Reference to these customs brings back worth-while historic references to the workings of this remarkable institution we call parliament. May I say in the house what I have often said outside, that I do not think that in the long history of mankind an institution has yet been devised which is as efficient and useful for the self-government of nations as is the parliamentary institution which we possess and under which we live


in this country. I think it is the duty of all members of the House of Commons to maintain respect for this institution.
With regard to the rules, I agree with the hon. member that the fewer rules we have the better it is for debate. When I came to the House of Commons some 20 years ago I expected to find the parliamentary rules being most carefully observed. I had taken part in debating clubs and societies and had belonged to organizations, including a city council, that had constitutions and bylaws, and when I came here I was amazed to find that strict parliamentary rules were more often disregarded than followed. I find that as a rule in smaller organizations that have constitutions and bylaws you are more apt to find the chairman enforcing the constitution and the rules with great vigour. As the hon. gentleman said, in this parliament of Canada there is across the floor of the house and from the Chair usually a breadth of tolerance which enables us to invoke the rules very rarely indeed.
With regard to the revision of the rules now before us, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said when the rules were introduced for consideration a short time ago, we carefully considered these amendments and accepted the package policy. That does not mean to say that we are entirely satisfied with all the proposed changes. I am sure the Leader of the Opposition will not misunderstand what I am about to say because I do not intend to cast any reflection upon him. In the recent debate I began to have some qualms about the 40-minute rule and about the new rule in connection with committees under which hon. members would be limited to 30 minutes.
I am not objecting to the 30-minute rule, which I think is a good rule, as I believe hon. members, except in exceptional circumstances, could condense their remarks and confine themselves to 20-minute speeches. Apparently they have no time limit in the British house, but I notice on reading their Hansard when there is an interesting debate that in the main most speeches run from 20 to 25 minutes. They seem to get along very well.
I think that if members of parliament are going to be limited to 40 minutes there should be some understanding regarding the length of time for which a member of the government or the Leader of the Opposition may speak. As I say, I am not reflecting upon anyone, but we did listen to a speech which taken in pieces extended for 4 hours and 20 minutes. Under the rules now laid before us the debate on particular topics is to be limited and the motions on going into

supply are to be limited also. If a member on the government side, a minister, say, occupies two to three hours in bringing something in and talking on a particular measure, and on our side of the house we have a speech of two to three hours or more, it means that private members of the house who are neither members of the government or leader of the opposition are going to be denied the right to enter the discussion in a particular debate. Consequently I would say this. We are going to accept the amendments as they are now before us because we have already pledged ourselves to that, but there will undoubtedly be a move in this house to amend these rules further, limiting, we shall say, a member of the government introducing a measure to one hour and a reply from our side to one hour, if restraint is not exercised by those who have the privilege that the rules are going to give them in this house.
I want to say that very forthrightly, because I think somebody has to say it. I say it, not in any disrespect to anyone. Please do not misunderstand me. I say it because I think that otherwise there will grow up in this house something of an ill feeling, and I do not want to see that. We have always had, as the hon. member for Temiscouata has said, a pretty good feeling in all parts of the house. That was the main point that I really wanted to make in connection with the rules.
These amendments are new and we are going to see how they work. I am in agreement with the hon. member for Temiscouata in another sense too, when he speaks of the citations. I know that those who have written the books of rules and procedures for us -Beauchesne, Bourinot, May and so on-have gone through the precedents of the past and have gathered all the decisions of the various Speakers or the decisions of the house together in these books. I have often found since I have been here that it is quite easy to find one citation that will support the government in one respect and another citation that will show that the first citation is wrong. It seems to me that the citations need to be looked over and many of them swept out of the rule books used in the house. Some of them are in conflict. As the hon. member said, some of them are entirely out of date. I think we need a committee to go into the rule books and see what can be eliminated from them.
In the same way, we have Speakers' decisions quoted as precedents. It seems to me that a Speaker's decision is the decision of the Speaker of the house at the time and that it should not be used to govern the house in all
Special Committee on Procedure subsequent sessions, as is sometimes the case. One of the reservations I always have when a decision of Mr. Speaker is challenged, in voting for or against the Speaker's ruling, is that once the house makes a decision in support of a Speaker's ruling it can be quoted as a very convenient precedent, even though the ruling may appear subsequently to have been wrong and not in the interests of the house itself.
I do not want to prolong the debate. I want to follow my own particular advice, which is to speak within 20 minutes or so on a matter. As a matter of fact, in the 20 years I have been here I do not think I have exceeded the 40-minute rule more than half a dozen times, because I think we should all try to live within the confines of the rules of debate. The 30-minute rule in committee is to be commended, and I would like to have seen that 30-minute rule put into effect in the major debates in the house, because the 30-minute rule would give more members an opportunity of expressing themselves. If everybody takes 40 minutes, you are going to deny some of the members the right to express themselves.
I think a good job has been done by the committee. While, as I say, I have some qualms about some of the proposals, none the less I think it is in the interests of parliament to try them out. When we have tried them out, we can set up a committee again and perhaps make some further revisions in the interests of facilitating the business of the house and at the same time preserving the rights of all members of the house.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take just a few minutes to speak on the matter which is now before the house. I am very glad that, as the result of two years of work, the special committee in this house was able to come to an agreement. It has been called a package deal but it is acceptable to all parties in this house, although everyone may not agree with everything that is in it.
There is, however, just one point on which I should like to speak. That is not so much as a criticism of the recommendations that have been made, but as a warning on a matter which I think we have to watch very carefully when we are changing any of the rules of this house and in the administration and the operation of the rules as they are adopted. I believe most sincerely that it is the duty of all the members so to watch the making of rules and the administration of the rules that we do not have a tendency to add to the powers of cabinet government.
I believe that in the past there has been, both in the legislatures and in the House of
5988	HOUSE OF
Special Committee on Procedure Commons, too great a tendency to increase the powers of cabinet government. Every time that is done we are getting away from the supremacy of parliament. I have always been interested in this matter, and a few weeks ago I had the opportunity of reading a book written by a man named MacKay, entitled "The Unreformed Senate of Canada-Constitutional and Political Limits". I should like to quote from one paragraph of that book, which reads as follows:
Canada is governed by two legislatures, one real, the other sham. The sham legislature is composed of the Governor General, the Senate and the House of Commons. The real legislature consists of a despotic ruler-the Premier; an Upper House-the Cabinet; and a Lower House-the caucus of the government members of parliament.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext: They do not have that any more.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
There is a great deal of truth in that paragraph, although it may not have applied in a recent decision of the government. In general it is true, and we have to be very careful to see that this cabinet power is not extended or their existing powers abused. I am interested in one particular phase of parliamentary procedure, and that is the powers and rights of the private members of the House of Commons. It is expressed in better words than I myself can bring to mind, in an article which I was reading the other day and which goes back quite a long time. The article is entitled "The Power of the Premier", and is contained in a publication called The News, published in the city of Toronto. The date of the publication is 28th November, 1905. I find it most interesting. This is what it says:
The supremacy of the cabinet has revolutionized the character of parliament. Not the least of the changes it has wrought has been the usurpation by the government of the time at the disposal of the private member for the initiation of legislation. It has been a maxim since the beginning of cabinet government that the cabinet is solely responsible for all administrative acts and all public expenditure. No other committee of parliament, no private member can be held politically responsible for either; t . decline of the power of the private member to put through such legislation is the result;
I was most interested in that quotation, Mr. Chairman, or in that statement made in 1905. I therefore went to the trouble of trying to find out just what has taken place in this House of Commons. I have here what I consider to be a most interesting chart. It is a list of all the acts initiated by the House of Commons from the session in 1924 until the session of 1953 inclusive. I find that from 1924 until 1953 the House of Commons has initiated and passed 1,799 bills. Of those 1,799 bills that were initiated in the House of Commons, only 33 were public bills introduced by private members. Of those 33,


three were amended by the Senate, 10 were rejected by the Senate and two were either withdrawn or action was not concluded. What that actually means is that out of 1,799 bills that were initiated in the House of Commons from 1924 to 1953 inclusive, only 21 bills of a public nature, introduced by private members, became the law of the Dominion of Canada.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext: That figure of 1,799 could not have included private bills.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext: That figure of 1,799 includes, government bills and private bills or public bills introduced by private members.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext: It could not include divorce bills.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
Divorce bills must have
greatly exceeded that number.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext: Oh, yes. I am speaking of public bills introduced in the House of Commons.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext: The other is private business.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
I personally think that 21 is a rather low figure in that period of time out of that number of bills. There are others who think that it is rather heavy. However, my point is this, Mr. Chairman. Whether the government like it or not, in the main the bills which finally become law are the result of the speaking of private members on the principle of bills or on the need for bills; and even although they are perhaps defeated year after year after year, the fact that they are introduced in principle or as public bills in the hands of private members ultimately results in government action. The introduction of new and progressive ideas and the demonstration of the need for new laws nearly always-not always but in the majority of cases-I think you will find, comes from the initiative of private members and also, to a great extent, comes from the ranks of the opposition whose job it is to criticize the government in a constructive manner and to put forward new ideas. I think it is most important that the attitude of the government toward the administration of the rules of this house should be such as not to put too great a limitation on the speaking rights of private members with regard to initiation of their ideas and putting forward public bills introduced by private members.
Of course I am going to support the motion which is now before the committee, but I wanted to point out the importance of private members and the importance of restraining

the power of cabinet government of which we have too much at the present time.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this report affords an opportunity for parliament to speak of itself. Only recently I was reading Quintin Hogg's book on parliament which sets forth something of the tradition, the ancient glory, and the modern power of parliament to maintain and to preserve freedom. 1 am going to quote just a few lines from that book:
Parliament is not like a building designed and constructed by a single architect, such as the Parthenon, St. Paul's cathedral and the Empire State building. Parliament resembles rather an ancient family mansion which has been lived in continuously for a period of centuries, and has served the needs of those who have dwelt therein by constantly modifying and adding to its conveniences from generation to generation.
Then a little bit later on:
To those who live in it, it is a priceless possession not to be exchanged for anything more meretricious and unified but those who are unfamiliar with its history are sometimes apt to lose themselves in its winding corridors and to be surprised and trapped by floors built at different times and on separate levels.
As I listened to the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar as he reviewed some of those ancient traditions and usages, it occurred to me how necessary it is for those of us in parliament to know something of the traditions, the history and the glory of the past in order to appreciate the responsibilities and the opportunities of parliament in the present.
I am one of those who looked askance when this committee was set up, for press reports were to the effect that it was the intention of the members supporting the government to force through, by the engine of their majority, amendments to the rules. Those fears have not been maintained in the results that have been effected. To the committee must go the congratulations of parliament on the work it has done.
In some amendments I fear that there is a danger that the functions of the opposition will be restrained and restricted by the rules that are being brought in. I refer in particular to the time limit on motions on going into supply and also to the time limit on the reply to the speech from the throne. If in the debate on the reply to the speech from the throne the government chose to throw in its members alternately with opposition members, it would mean that the opposition would indeed be denied its right to speak and to advance its ideas.
After all, oppositions have their functions. What happened yesterday was an outstanding example of what an opposition can do in parliament. An opposition is restricted to its
12, 1955
Special Committee on Procedure right to speak and to protest, and to public opinion being created. Governments, however powerful, must bend to public opinion as represented by those who speak in opposition with authority and with responsibility. However, taking the recommendations in general, my opinion is that the committee has laid the foundations for a better and more efficient House of Commons, and it is our responsibility to make parliament efficient. The hon. member who preceded me mentioned the decline in the power of private members. That is all too true. Read Hansard of 50 and 60 years ago and see there the degree to which the leaders of parliament-I refer not to those in authority but to those leaders in debate-moved the people by their erudition, their wisdom and their statesmanship with responsibility. No one wants to go back to the days of 70 years ago when debate was unlimited. An example of that is to be found in Hansard in 1885 when the Saskatchewan Riel rebellion was being discussed. Speaking now from recollection, I think the first three speakers spoke from five to seven hours. One spoke for eight hours. Sir John A. Macdonald felt he could cover the situation and answer the arguments of the then opposition in a speech which he confined and repressed to five hours and 16 minutes. Those were the days when lengthy speeches were of the essence of debate.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext: Sermons were the same length.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
The sermons, of course, sometimes had a text. However, the right to speak at length must be inherent in parliament. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar mentioned the British parliament. There there is no limitation except that required and demanded by the exigencies of the debate. In the congress of the United States the reading of speeches became so general that the inevitable followed and speakers simply filed and tabled their speeches. That is one of the things we have to guard against in this house, for if the tendency of members to read speeches continues then sooner or later we are going to be placed in the position where we must inevitably follow the United States system. When that is followed parliamentary debate ceases and parliament will no longer be the institution that parliament should be.
I think one of the reasons for lengthy speeches today in those parliaments that are modelled after the British parliamentary system but do not follow it exactly is to be found in the presence of desks. In the British House of Commons there are no desks. No longer can one suggest abolishing desks, but

Special Committee on Procedure it is interesting to note that all over the commonwealth wherever desks are to be found in parliamentary institutions debates do not have that succinctness, clarity and distinction which exists under the British parliamentary system. It would be the heresy of all time for me to suggest the removal of desks today, but I do think that the removal of the desks would improve the quality of debate in the House of Commons and parliament beyond the imagination of any of us.
Wherever one goes in the commonwealth one finds the same arguments advanced that we hear here. It is said that parliament is speaking at too great length. There is not the study of the subjects upon which speeches are made that there should be. Remove the desks and the result is a vast increase in diligence of preparation and in the study of the subject. Debates in the British parliament are not lengthy with the exception of the historic debates of 1910 and 1911 when Lloyd George was anathema throughout the length and breadth of the United Kingdom. Those debates were lengthy debates because there was an abiding principle at stake.
The same thing took place in our own country during the naval debates. As a youngster I sat in the gallery of the House of Commons and listened to those debates. I often recall the greatness of those days. One thinks of the Lauriers and the Bordens, and one could name other great speakers of that time who carried on debate for weeks on end, as a debate was recently carried on, for whenever the privileges and traditions of parliament are invaded parliament should be vocal.
As I said a moment ago, the new rules do not change to any great extent the rights of the opposition and of parliament in general. They represent a compromise. A compromise is never perfect but compromise is of the essence of parliamentary discussion and deliberation. Mention was made by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and I think also by the hon. member for Temiscouata about the application of the rule of stare decisis to Speakers' decisions. I am opposed to that. I think nothing will emasculate parliament more than for it to be imprisoned by decisions made by Speakers without that consideration that cannot always be given. In any event, such decisions apply only to the events of the moment and should not become authoritative and binding on subsequent Speakers, for after all the rules are made for the purpose of ensuring orderly debate. We do not want to turn parliament into an afternoon society meeting. If we have strong opinions we want to express them. We do not want to engage in personalities as such, but if we allow our rules or Speakers' decisions to place members of parliament in the position where if they
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
use a strong expression they have to withdraw it parliament will become nothing but a mere debating society.
After all, strong men have strong opinions. I think our trend in the last 15 or 20 years has been to reduce the standard of debate in parliament by the insistence on the letter of decorum. We do not carry our ill feelings outside of the House of Commons, and the things that we say, as long as they do not impute personal wrongdoing or lack of integrity, should be permitted in the House of Commons.
If we come to the point where every little expression of criticism results in a request for withdrawal, then indeed will parliament cease to maintain the traditions of the days of Sir John A. Macdonald, D'Arcy McGee, Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Blake. They spoke strongly. Yes, in the days of Borden, Mackenzie King and Arthur Meighen, they spoke strongly. I often wonder, if they came back to parliament today and were to see the restrictions that the accumulation of rules has made on debate, whether they would recognize it as the place where they achieved their glories and where freedom was maintained.
I believe that in essence, Mr. Chairman, the rules as amended will be effectual in that the anachronisms and paradoxes of past rules have been removed. While there has been a diminution in the speaking time in committee, in reality that diminution is not going to reduce the time for debate or render ineffectual the opportunities for criticism. I welcome the changes that have brought about the removal of unnecessary, inapplicable and paradoxical rules of the past. I think that the committee, in what it has done, will at least have achieved a modicum of advance in parliamentary debate.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that the house will welcome the report that is before us. For several sessions now, the house has been attempting to arrive at some satisfactory and unanimous agreement to bring up to date the rules governing the procedure of this house. We have had committees working on this in previous sessions, but evidently at this session we have arrived somewhere. I wish to say now that we in this group appreciate the work of this committee. I think I should hand my colleague a little bouquet. Our party whip, as our representative on that committee, I believe did some substantial work. Every week, he would report to us as a group concerning the progress that had been made, thus keeping us well informed. Each week we made our

suggestions to him and eventually arrived at a unanimous decision that our party would support this report.
There are, however, some things upon which perhaps we, as individuals, would like to express ourselves, even though not in opposition to the report. As I say, we appreciate the report and have adopted it unanimously. The problem that seemed to be facing us was that there was a general desire to streamline the procedure of parliament. There was a feeling here, and a feeling in the country too because I have received this impression from other people apart from parliament but people who are vitally interested in the activities of parliament, that our present rules of procedure were somewhat antiquated. There was a feeling we had not quite kept pace with the advanced age and were still running parliament on the basis of what might be termed a more or less antiquated system of procedure.
The problem the committee had to meet was how to streamline parliamentary procedure to make parliament more efficient, while at the same time retaining what we believed to be a very important heritage, that is our democratic processes. I feel we have made progress in that respect. I do not think we have denied, to any great extent, the democratic rights of members of parliament, and yet have made some progress with regard to the streamlining of our procedure; although I will say that we have not gone too far. Progress along the lines of parliamentary procedure must be attained over a long period of time, and must be attained step by step. We cannot rush into something and then find we have made the mistake of going too far. Rules should be revised from time to time gradually, without interfering with our democratic processes.
I would suggest this, Mr. Chairman, that we must always recognize that we sit here as members of parliament representing the people of Canada and as individuals representing the people of a certain area. We call them constituencies. When we come here, we come here to speak on behalf of the people. I like to think of parliament as a place where we are all equal. It is for that reason I agree with one of the previous speakers that we must oppose cabinet administration and its power over parliament. It has no place in our democratic way of life. We are not elected in reality on the basis of parties. I know we go to the electors as parties because we believe in certain tenets of political doctrine, and because we believe in those we band ourselves together to make proposals to the people and present ourselves for election. I suppose to that extent
12, 1955
Special Committee on Procedure we are aligned with a party which believes certain political doctrines.
But we are not in reality elected as party members. We are elected as individuals representing the people of the areas from which we come or where we stand for election. I feel I can say that is so by reason of the fact that not so long ago-I do not want to become confused in this matter-one of our members presented a private bill to amend the elections act so that the name on the ballot would contain also the party for which the person is running. We think that is a good idea, but the house turned that down. They may have had a particular reason for turning that one down, but I think basically the reason that it has not been done over the years is that members run as representatives of the people.
Not so long ago a rather distinguished gentleman of the press gallery wrote a book, the title of which was "The People's Mouths". Of course, it was a book on members of parliament. Many members of parliament were mentioned by name. Of course, the title carries with it a very strong significance; that is, that we are here as the people's mouths. The people as a whole have no possible practical way of coming before the throne and making a complaint. What do they do? They elect somebody as a member of a constituted body known as parliament in which they can speak and lay their complaints at the foot of the throne. Therefore, when we come and speak we speak on behalf of the people whom we represent. We are their mouths before the throne. That traditionally and basically is the reason for parliament. Therefore, what I would say in that respect is that all members are equal here, and there should be no curtailing of their rights to speak, because if there is any curtailment of the rights of a member to speak, then what are we doing? We are curtailing the right of the people to express themselves through the person whom they have elected to speak for them. That is very basic and very fundamental, and therefore in all the streamlining of parliament we must preserve and protect the traditional rights of the people as expressed through their members.
Take the matter of the curtailment of time. I wondered at first whether it was a good idea to cut the length of the debate on the speech from the throne and the budget to so many days, because I felt that abuses could be made in that respect, even though there may be a sort of gentleman's agreement that the government side of the house will not take undue time. We are relying on that gentleman's agreement. I do not think I would have approved of that suggestion had

Special Committee on Procedure it not been for the fact that the same rule does not apply to bills or estimates. I could see a way by which, if the government side of the house took advantage of that ruling and filled the program for those days with their own speakers, thus limiting the time of the house for other groups in the house, we would reasonably say, all right, we shall catch up with you when our time comes, and when the estimates or some bills come up we can catch up and take all the time we wish to take.
There is another thing, too, in that respect. I do not know where independent members would fit into this picture. Remember, they, as independents, represent their people just as much as the prime minister or a cabinet minister or some distinguished member of one of the major parties. They have just as much right here and just as much right to speak as anyone else. I do not like to imply that the Speakers, those gentlemen of honour who occupy the Speaker's chair, would take any advantage. I am sure they would not. I can say this to Your Honour, the Deputy Speaker of this house, and to Mr. Speaker himself. Every hon. member would agree that you are among the fairest gentlemen who have occupied those positions. In fact, on some occasions, I can say that you have tried to help us out if we reached a little bit of an impasse, and have gone the extra mile to accommodate us. I am sure we appreciate that. While I am saying that, I should like to say the same thing about the deputy chairman of committees, our good friend the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite), who also sometimes occupies the chair as Acting Speaker. He is most generous. I am sure we appreciate your actions. But I do not know that I can say that of every Speaker who has occupied the chair. In my experience in this house over the last 20 years I do not know that I can say that. I am not going to mention any names, but I have often been tempted to rise in my place and ask whether Mr. Speaker's left eye was a glass eye, because it seemed to me on some occasions that the only people he could see were those he could see with his right eye. Of course, I did not do that. Perhaps there was a mote in it. Anyway, there is a possibility that an unfair Speaker could take advantage of a ruling of that kind and cut off the privileges and rights of members who sit on the opposition side of the house. I hope that never happens.
We do extend some courtesies to the prime minister; we extend courtesies to cabinet ministers and to the leader of the opposition when they want extended time for their speeches. I do believe that the leader of the
(Mr. Hansell.]
C.C.F. party, and the leader of this party, the Social Credit party, should also be given extended time if they are making a policy speech in some important debate. I am sure that the socialists feel that they have a philosophy that might be an alternative to the matters debated, and I am quite certain-and I do not think I would sit here tomorrow if I did not believe this-that the Social Credit party has an alternative to offer to the status quo and in fact to every other group. When it comes to presenting that alternative, with all its doctrinaire applications, the leader of the group should be given extended time as well as the opposition leader, the prime minister and those of cabinet rank.
I have one or two other things to say, Mr Chairman. In the first place we must remember that parliament after all is a place where people talk. I remember on one occasion, when the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) was talking, someone shouted "Let's get on with the business; too mucu talk." The hon. member for Lethbridge said. "Well, what are we here for if it is not to talk?" That is a very pertinent question. What are we here for if it is not to talk? After all, the very word "parliament" comes from "parley," a gathering together in a place to talk. That is what it means.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext: To say something.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
Yes; it is a place in which to say something as well as to talk. Of course, there may be variations as to what is meant by talk. It is a place to talk and furthermore when we talk it is recorded by these gentlemen who work so hard and who are called Hansard reporters. They do a marvellous job of reporting what is said, a better job sometimes than by other types of reporters. I know the press wants to be fair, but sometimes when you read the papers it is hard to detect whether the reports were made up from what was said here or from what somebody told them was said here. I have no criticism in that respect, but I do say that Hansard is the only official document setting out what has been said in the highest court of the land.
It is the only document of an authoritative nature which reports what has been said in a place where men are free to speak. We are more free to say things here than they are any place else in the world. It is one place which cannot be touched by any other court. It is one place where the people's mouths are free to say what they want to say, and Hansard is the official record of what has been said. It is kept in the library of parliament over the centuries of time and is the official document. If we want proof

of what we have said we do not go to some magazine or newspaper, we go to the source of that authority.
I am saying these things only to indicate that when the people speak there should be no curtailment as to what they want to say or as to how long they want to take to say it. I agree that we have to enter into a gentleman's agreement, that we have to have some reasonable rules and therefore we have the rule that we shall speak for 40 minutes only. I often kick myself for taking more time than I need but I know I am long-winded. My leader has said that no one is ever convinced after the first 20 minutes anyway. I admit all that and I am quite certain that if I really disciplined myself I could say in 30 minutes what I usually take 40 minutes to say.
I am quite willing that speeches should be limited in time. I am not contradicting my own argument when I say that, I simply believe that most of us could confine ourselves to 30 minutes. However, we are allowed 40 minutes in the house and 30 minutes in committee where we can speak as often as we want to speak. I think that rule is a good one.
I have one or two trivial matters I want to refer to and I shall not take too much time in doing so. The first is the rule governing the reading of speeches. I know that that rule is most difficult to enforce and I know that you, Mr. Chairman, have had some experience along those lines and our sympathies are with you. I urge hon. members to discipline themselves in respect to the reading of speeches. After all, if this is a place of parley, if this is a place of talk, I do not see why a member should let his name stand for election if he cannot come down here and talk without reading from a manuscript.
Some very distinguished members of this house, men with a string of degrees, men connected with distinguished law firms never make speeches in this house without reading them. I do not think that that is right and it is something about which we should be checked up a little more. If an hon. member has a speech all typed out and is going to read it, why take up the time of the house in doing so. Why should not that hon. member be asked if he is reading his speech? Mr. Speaker could ask to see his notes and if it were clear that the member was using a manuscript Mr. Speaker could rule that it be placed on Hansard and the floor could be given to those who wanted to speak instead of reading speeches. It would all be in Hansard just the same.

We get into the habit of waiting for the bells to ring, then we pick up some books or letters or something else we may want to take with us or we chat with our secretaries or someone else and the first thing we know when we get down here we have to stand behind the curtain until the prayers are finished.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
There are some hon. members who never miss; they have disciplined themselves much more carefully than I have. I want to make a little suggestion. I suggest that about five minutes before the time for Your Honour to enter the chamber there should be a short ring of the bells for about three or four seconds. Then when Mr. Speaker enters the chamber about five minutes later the bells would ring in the regular way. That might encourage some laziness on the part of hon. members, but it might be well to try that for a while in order to have more hon. members here for prayers.
The prayers we hear at the opening of our sessions offer great encouragement in our democratic way of life and the carrying on of our duties in this parliament. I have sent copies of our prayers to many people. I believe the prayers that are read here, one day in English and one day in French, are classics of literature and of Christian doctrine. I do not know their history but I understand that a committee met many years ago and designed the prayer. The members of that committee must have been inspired. I certainly would not want to see that prayer changed.
I think I have taken up enough time and I close with saying that we are in support of this report.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the procedure of the house is one of the most serious responsibilities we have. In revising

Special Committee on Procedure our rules it is most important that we keep in mind the rights of the individual, the purposes of members of parliament, and the purposes of the opposition. I hope that in revising our rules we are never guilty of curtailing or in any way curbing the democratic rights of the people and their representatives in the house. I think we can all agree that revision of the house rules in this case was necessary and what the committee has done meets generally with the approval of most parties. The representatives of each of the various parties in the house who were chosen to act on the committee in the house have in general done a very good job. As the representative from this group said on the 1st of July:
As the hon. member for Kamloops has said, this does not mean that every individual in each of the four parties has to support every item in the report.
There may be objections to some of the rules because it may be felt that there is some curtailment of the democratic rights of an individual. There is one feature of the amendment to which I wish as an individual to raise some objection. That is the curtailment of the time being given to the debate on the speech from the throne. Therefore every individual in this house elected by the people in his constituency could say he had the undeniable right to stand up at some time during that debate and place before the throne the situation with regard to his constituency. It is my contention that by limiting the debate to 10 days, you might possibly be curtailing that right. Heretofore the government back-bench members have largely refrained from the debate. They have taken up very little time in the debate. Most of the time in the throne speech debate has been occupied by members of the various opposition groups.
The opposition has a very important function to perform in parliament and there should be nothing that could curtail the right of the opposition to speak. I maintain that, by limiting that to 10 days as has been done in these rules, you might curtail the right of an individual member-perhaps not of the official opposition, perhaps not of our group, perhaps not of the Social Credit group, perhaps a member of the independent group. If a large number of government members spoke for their 40 minutes within the 10 days, the time might be used up for members speaking, and then the debate would be closed. I say it is possible. A member might then say, "I am denied that opportunity now;
I shall have an opportunity on the budget debate." But again in the revision of standing order No. 57C it says:
The proceedings on the order of the day for resuming debate on the motion "That Mr. Speaker


do now leave the chair" for the house to resolve itself into committee of ways and means (budget) and on any amendments proposed thereto shall not exceed eight sitting days.
Again, in one of the main omnibus debates in which a member is allowed to bring in any matter of difficulty in his constituency, he is curtailed. That is limited to eight days. I am not saying that that will happen, but I do say that under the amended rules that can happen. If that can happen, then I think we are losing something. That is the one objection I wish to register against these amendments. The opposition has a purpose to perform. In Robert MacGregor Dawson's book "The Government of Canada", he quotes W. S. Moncrieff favourably, on page 447:
The house meets, and in march the opposition, and sit there ready to attack ministers and their measures; never, if possible, to make a concession, by word or vote, to official shrewdness or skill. For the time being they are Her Majesty's loyal sappers and miners, not to be very particular if only they can hack and hew their way to the treasury benches. They are waiters upon Providence-all animated with the most exalted, never-say-die, patriotism. If they only had a bandage on their brow inscribed, "organized fault-finders," and a symbolical grid-iron, to be transferable, like the seals of office, the equipment would be complete. Broiling is a part of their special functions; and woe to the minister when a chief, with the spirit of an untamed Indian, is at the head of his foes. For party aims, he is understood to be clothed with forked-lightning invectives; and in debate, wonder not if he substitutes epithets for arguments, and deals more with the motives than the logic of ministers. In brief, he and his lieutenants must be quick to detect the joints in the armour of those in power; and, above everything, they are bound to cultivate the most wakeful and morbid suspiciousness."
The duty of the opposition to carry that out must not be curtailed. I maintain that in the amendment to the rules proposed here the possibility of that denial exists in the limitation of the debate. There is no limitation today in the speeches on the throne speech debate. There is no particular curtailment in committee. There is no curtailment in the speeches on estimates. But there is curtailment proposed in those omnibus debates which, I maintain, could be a denial of opportunity to a member to speak.
In general, with the rules as they exist today and with the alertness that I see in this house today, I think the members of this house would be conscious of the fact that a member's right might be curtailed. I am personally of the belief that, so long as we have in parliament men who are alert and alive to the rights of democracy and the rights of individual members to speak and to carry out their functions as an opposition, and the realization that the opposition is here to find fault with the government and to keep the government alert, democracy is safe. The fact that the opposition is doing

that tends to make good government. We would be wise to keep that purpose in mind in amending the rules.
I would say that parliament as it exists today in Canada is an institution of which Canadians can be proud. It is important that it be maintained as such. I think the one weakness in these amendments is that there is the possibility of denial of the right of a member representing the people to speak, through the double curtailment. I would support wholeheartedly the limitation of eight days of the debate on the budget, but I believe it is weakening this house as a democratic institution to curtail both of those debates. I would support one or the other, but I cannot support the curtailment of both.
I would suggest that the first amendment, the one to the throne speech debate, is the one where we have erred. That is the new standing order 38A. Every member should be able to say to the people of his constituency, who have elected him, "I went to the House of Commons and I was never denied the right to present the situation of my constituents, at the foot of the throne".
May I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, prior to the lunch hour I was outlining some of the reasons why I could not agree with the changes that are being proposed in the report of the special committee on the procedure of the House of Commons. The house committee which drafted the report had on it able representatives and there apparently was towards the end fairly general agreement. My objection is to the fact that there is to be a curtailment of one of the debates, something which is new to Canadian parliamentary procedure. I refer to the fact that the debate on the speech from the throne has been curtailed to a 10-day period.
During the lunch hour someone asked me how it was that I maintained that this rule is going to prevent members from speaking. It gives them 10 days. The days are being made longer. We are going to have morning sittings and therefore, they say, it is going to amount to the same thing, probably about 14 or 15 days anyway. I said: Oh yes, but this is the difference. If the government with its overwhelming majority permits the backbenchers to speak in any large number, instead of using about 20 per cent of the time as they do at the present time, they will be 50433-379J
Special Committee on Procedure taking up 60 per cent or even 80 per cent of the time, which will leave about 20 per cent to the opposition. If that 20 per cent of the time is all that the opposition has out of those 10 days, and if you split that up among the various groups, the three or four parties, you can easily see what could happen. If we try to ration that time there will be disagreement between the official opposition-the Progressive Conservatives-the Co-operative Commonwealth group, the Social Credit group and the independent members at the end of the chamber here. With the difference in the numbers, I do not know how we are possibly going to come to an agreement. Does that mean that this will cause friction between these parties? Perhaps the government would like that but I doubt whether it is good for parliament. If the time which the opposition at present uses is 80 per cent of those 12 days, and that time is cut down to only 20 per cent of the 12 days, I maintain that the opportunity for members of the opposition to speak will be curtailed or will be cut into one-quarter of that which they are using at the present time. The possibility of that event happening is the thing to which we should object.
The right of a minority group or of an individual to speak in this house should not be a matter of struggle. His right to speak for his constituents should be an undenied right which, when he comes here representing the people of any constituency, he knows is inherent in the fact that he was elected. We should make doubly sure that that right should never be denied him. It is to the possibility of that right being denied him that we raise objection.
The rules of the house are the bulwarks of that right or the very basis upon which that right is protected. It is behind these rules that the right of democracy exists. I maintain that in this matter we are weakening those bulwarks. The duty of members of parliament is to protect democracy. Rather than weakening these bulwarks we should be strengthening them.

Westminster is a fine example. A large number of members sit in their house. Their house sits continuously all the year round. They have their recesses or holidays. The business of the whole of the 55 million people of that country-and a great country it is-constituting an important

Special Committee on Procedure part of the picture of the world, with a great deal of business to do-is conducted there. They sit continuously. Unfortunately there are only 365 days in the year. Their motion to adjourn at night is quite frequently wiped away and they sit all night. Quite frequently they sit until six o'clock or seven o'clock in the morning.

speechtext: And use closure twice a week.

maintopic: SECOND REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE-CONSIDERATION IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
speechtext:
Conditions are quite different. As has been outlined here today, there are differences in the situation here from that in the house at Westminster. Somebody spoke about the United States and said that members of congress are allowed to speak for any length of time. I believe the record in the United States senate is something like 23 hours and 20 minutes. I believe that one man held the floor for that period of time. Here we have our rules curtailing speakers to 30 minutes or 40 minutes.
Let us not in Canada deny to members of parliament the right to speak. We have the time in which to do the business of the house. We have the time in which to do the business of the country. Members of parliament are well paid to do that job. They should be here and they should be doing it. Ask the people of Canada whether they want the rights of members of parliament curtailed, and find out what they want.
I can realize that members of the cabinet are men who want to get business done. I can understand that desire in men coming from successful walks of life in the business world. I can understand it, for instance, in a man who has made a success in the engineering line, whose whole training from his youth up has been a matter of getting a job done well and getting it done within certain limitations of time. That is the way he makes his money. There is a deadline. He has to meet it. If the thing cannot be done within that specified time, then move things out of the way in order to get it done.
In these days it is important that the business of government be done on time. For that reason we give to these ministers special powers. In wartime or time of emergency we grant them special powers because such powers allow them to do important business within the time in which it is required to be done for the safety of the nation. But that should not be a basis or a reason for the government to deny to members of parliament the democratic right of speaking for their constituencies. I believe that we are weakening that democratic right if we accept this proposal.

The consideration of efficiency in getting important business of government done on time should not interfere with the democratic process. Otherwise we are weakening it. It is because of the possible curtailment of the right of a representative chosen by the people in any constituency in any part of Canada to express the opinions which he was elected to express, and to express them clearly in this house, that I raise this objection. It is to prevent the possibility of that change that I oppose this amendment or what is proposed in the amendment. I still maintain-and will continue to do so-that the right, at least once in Canada's parliament, should be maintained for an individual member to rise and speak in an omnibus debate and to say those things which his constituents elected him to say. Canada's parliament should never deny that right to any person whom Canadians have elected and sent to this house.
