I should like to ask the minister regarding the plans for the development and improvement at Wolseley barracks, London. Would he outline the new construction and installations which are planned, what the proposed expenditure will be for this year and the next four years, and how much is proposed to be spent during the fiscal year? Will he indicate how much will be spent during the next four years? Is it planned to acquire any further property adjacent to what is now known as Wolseley barracks in Carling Heights? Is it planned to increase the amount of space allotted for married quarters now or in the immediate future?

All these questions have to do with the Canadian army, regular, the estimates for which we have passed. I have no desire, however, to refuse information, but it will take some time to get the figures requested. As the hon. member knows we are establishing a home station at London which involves a great deal of construction, a large part of which is in progress and the remainder of which will be initiated in coming years. I have no objection to giving what figures I can, but it will take some little time to obtain them.

Just before the committee rose I had asked the minister about the arrangements in effect at defence headquarters for the organization and training of the militia. The minister stated that General Letson had

been appointed recently as special officer in charge of militia, and that Colonel Buell had been named as well. Could I ask what qualifications of training and experience Colonel Buell has?

Colonel Buell is a regular officer who has served with distinction with the Canadian army for a good many years. As a matter of fact I think he is the son of Colonel Buell of Vancouver, whom the hon. member may know, who was very active in the first world war. Colonel Buell has also been director of cadet training for some years.
In answer to the whole question raised by the hon. member, as I stated yesterday we have General Letson as adviser on militia matters to the chief of the general staff. We also have Colonel Buell, to whom I have just referred, as director of militia and of cadets.
Each branch and directorate at headquarters has the responsibility for the militia as well as the regular army as part of its normal function. In other words the several branches of headquarters deal not only with the regular army but with the militia as well. For example, the directorate of military training establishes training policy standards for both the regular army and the militia. The staffs at command and area headquarters are responsible for the supervision, administration and training of militia units and, in particular, the administration and arrangement of annual camps and courses conducted throughout the area for the militia. In addition the regular army renders such assistance as is practicable to militia units in the various commands throughout the country.
Permanent assistance to the militia is provided by an instructional cadre on a command pool basis, and the establishment of this cadre, which is available for militia purposes, is approximately 700 officers and men located throughout the country. Following the recommendation of the Kennedy committee, authority has been granted for the employment on a full-time basis of 536 militia personnel to perform administrative duties at the various militia units. Working through militia group headquarters, of which I think there are 25, these men assist in the co-ordination of activities in the particular areas for which they are responsible. That may indicate the tie-up that exists between headquarters staffs and the commands throughout the country, in relation to the training of militia as connected with the army regiments.

I do not think the minister gave us the arm in which Colonel Buell served.
Supply-National Defence
Infantry.

That is a very good qualification. Would the minister give us a little more detail, please, as to the tasks to be performed by General Letson and Colonel Buell? Are they to be purely in an advisory capacity to the chief of the general staff, or do they have any direct control in an administrative sense of the militia?
Mr Campney: I believe General Letson acts wholly in an advisory capacity on militia to the chief of the general staff. Colonel Buell is charged with administrative duties both in respect to militia and in respect to cadets.

What I would be anxious to know is the relationship between the functions of Colonel Buell and those of the various branches of the permanent army at headquarters here, which the minister told us a moment ago also had responsibilities in connection with the militia. Could the minister give us more detail as to whether Colonel Buell's main job is to co-ordinate the activities of the various branches of the permanent forces with respect to the militia or merely to advise them on it, and what staff does he have? I realize that this is perhaps in the developmental stage, but how is it envisaged as working? In other words, I should like to be assured that this is not merely another gesture-and I use the term with respect-but that something concrete is going to come out of this.

Colonel Buell, who devotes his full time to his directorate of militia and cadets, is in a large degree a co-ordinator. He visits units, studies their needs and brings those needs to the attention of the various directorates of the army interested in particular matters. So his duties are much more than advisory. He has executive duties, and he has access to the other directorates of the army to make known the needs of the militia in an endeavour to have them met. He also advises other directorates on matters he thinks should be brought to their attention in the best interests of the militia. So in every sense of the word he is a very active and practical head of a directorate, similar to the heads of the other directorates of the army.
Is that directorate of equal status to the other directorates?
Yes, it has equal status with the directorate of infantry and the other directorates.

I believe the minister said
there are approximately 700 personnel of the permanent force assigned as a training cadre and 536 militia personnel whose employment

Supply-National Defence on a full-time basis has been authorized. That makes a total of approximately 1,236. Can the minister give us a more concrete figure as to the total number of personnel who would be engaged in the administration, training and organization of the militia? I do not mean the militia themselves. I am trying to get the size of the effort being devoted, here at national defence headquarters and in the army throughout Canada, to the establishment, organization and training of the militia.

In addition to the personnel of the directorate of militia, as I mentioned, all the directorates and their personnel devote whatever time may be required from time to time to militia activities. They are all charged with accepting whatever duties are brought to their attention within their respective directorates for the benefit of the militia. In other words the attempt was made-and I think it is meeting with a very high degree of success-to develop the militia training and administration, by having its directorate brought into correlation with other army directorates and their personnel.
Of course, the 536 full-time militia personnel allocated to militia operations were also the product of the Kennedy committee. They provide a connecting link of a military nature between militia units and headquarters, and reduce a good deal the delays and paper work ordinarily necessary. That also, I think, has more than justified itself so far as it has been tried. We are still tidying up the organization, but I think it is one step that has been extremely useful.

Would it be correct to say that there are in round figures only these 1,200 personnel whose duties are exclusively related to the militia, and that the others have a dual function; that is to say they are administering the permanent forces and discharging such duties as are entrusted to them with respect to the militia?
I would say that is a fair statement of the position.

With respect to the director of the militia, can the minister say whether he has direct chain of command or authority to the militia units, or does he have in every respect to transmit instructions through the area commands?
All instructions-and that includes those from director of militia-go through command and area headquarters. The same procedure is followed in respect of the militia or any other units of the army.

So the organization for the militia is from units, from area headquarters,
rMr. Fulton. 1
to the director. It is difficult to get this matter into watertight compartments, but what authority does the director have in relation to the area headquarters? Can he issue instructions and require certain things to be done, or does he have to go perhaps through General Letson to the chief of the staff and make recommendations to him, and does the order have to be transmitted down from the chief of staff and through these channels out to area headquarters?

I should say that the chain of responsibilities varies. If it is a matter of policy, then it would go, I presume, from General Letson to the chief of the general staff and be dealt with as would any other matter of policy. If it were a purely administrative matter, then I think he has sufficient authority, as do the other directors in their own respective spheres, to deal directly with the units through command and through area. It would depend on the nature of the particular item as to the way in which it was done.
What staff has this directorate at the moment? What is the total number of personnel in that directorate?
Altogether I think there are 12 or 15, approximately that number, including two lieutenant colonels and six other officers, plus personnel of lower rank.

Can the minister just give us an indication of the nature of the organization of that directorate and of its various components? I do not mean that the minister give it to us person by person, but rather that he give us an outline of its organization.

As I understand it, the directorate is divided into two subdivisions, each of which is headed by a lieutenant colonel. One division deals with militia units and militia matters and the other division of the directorate deals with cadets, of which we have about 65,000 at the present time.
How long has it been established now?
Almost a year; it was established as soon as it could be put into effect after the report was examined and accepted by the chief of the general staff, and by the minister.

Some question was asked earlier which related to this matter. I think it would be helpful if the minister could give us the percentage of those training with the militia units throughout Canada who will go to camp this summer for annual training.

I think I gave the figure last night. If I recollect correctly the present strength of the militia is roughly 45,000. Yes

the figure which I gave was as of April 20, 1955, 45,828. The estimated number of those who are attending or who will be attending camp during the present year-we have not the actual figures yet, of course-is 19,082. That was the estimate that was made at the beginning of December of the number who would go to camp.

I can only express some regret that at this stage of these estimates we have not a clearer picture of what has been taking place. Questions have been asked with regard to tank training, anti-tank training and the training of the units generally. I think it is agreed by everyone that in this country the militia is the backbone of our army organization. It is from the militia, in large measure, that enlistment comes in the permanent units.
I think it would be unfortunate if anyone left the estimates at this time without recognizing that at a time when we are spending such enormous sums of money, there are practically no units of the militia in Canada that either are fully equipped or are equipped with the most modern weapons. The question must be in the minds of everyone as to what the concept of our militia is. I noticed a statement given to the press a few days ago by the department to the effect that the department was confronted with a great decision as to whether to concentrate on conventional or nuclear war. The fact is that even in relation to the conventional units we have, there is not any suggestion that those are units in being ready to take the field in the event of difficulties.
I think at this stage a word should be said about the magnificent contribution being made by the members of our militia units training for the defence of Canada. They are limited in numbers. They are limited in opportunity to get the complete training that some of us would wish them to have. But in spite of all that the officers, N.C.O.'s and men of our militia units have done a magnificent job within the limitations under which they are framing. I think their carriage on parade and their acceptance of the duties that fall upon them are a credit to every one of them.
However, if events are as serious as they are portrayed to us, and if the times call for the sense of emergency which has been emphasized on various occasions in recent weeks, I feel that we should decide that the time has come for our militia units to be much more comprehensively trained and equipped than has been true in recent years. Whether it is artillery, tanks or armoured units; whether it is infantry, the army service corps or other units of our army, we are still training them as though we were under severe
Supply-National Defence limitations while at the same time we are spending such tremendous sums of money.
I wish we could have a clearer picture; but even in the somewhat blurred picture that is presented one thing is not uncertain, and that is the splendid contribution that is being made by the volunteer members of our militia forces. I feel that all hon. members have reason for satisfaction that, under whatever difficulties or limitations there may be, they are showing the kind of spirit that has made the militia the backbone of our whole defence organization.

I should like to ask a brief question that relates to the armouries at Virden, Manitoba. About four years ago the Department of National Defence purchased the lot adjoining the armouries there. Since that time oil has been discovered in Virden. The population has doubled within two or three years and property, particularly in the main section of the town, is at a premium. The question has been asked, what does the Department of National Defence intend to do with the property adjoining the armouries there, which it has had in its possession for some four years now?

I am not aware of all the circumstances attending the acquisition of that property at Virden. I presume it must have been purchased for use in conjunction with or for extension of the armouries. I have not been able to make a review of the armouries situation this year yet, to see what armouries we may be able to build. As I mentioned the other evening, ever since Korea we have necessarily curtailed the construction of armouries because of lack of funds, but we are now making a study of the armouries situation in order to arrange priorities and make some disposition of the most urgent needs. When I am looking into the matter, as I hope to be very shortly, I shall look at the Virden situation. I am not familiar with the details at the moment.
I take it that it is contemplated there will be an extension of the armouries at Virden?

I cannot say that. Frankly I do not know because, as I say, we are just preparing now a study of the whole armouries situation to decide which are more urgently needed than others and within what financial limits we can construct armouries this year and in the years to come.

I should like, somewhat hesitantly, to express an opinion. I hardly even like to call it an opinion, but as a result of the answers the minister has given to my question about the directorate of the militia

Supply-National Defence I am concerned over the question of the chain of command and communication. I understand that for anything requiring a decision or anything in the way of an instruction of major importance, the chain would be from the director down through area and command headquarters and from there to the militia units. I presume if a request or recommendation were going in the reverse direction it would have to go from the unit through command and area headquarters up to the director, and for any decision to be taken the matter would have to go to the chief of staff. Then if a decision is taken it goes from him back down through the staff channels of area and command headquarters and so on.
I wonder whether that would not tend to have the result, since obviously the main concern of area and command headquarters is with the permanent force, that militia problems will tend to assume a secondary place and the giving and implementation of decisions with respect to the militia will become delayed. There is no direct or personal criticism of area and command staffs involved here, because we are dealing with human nature. They are permanent force officers and personnel, and that is their main responsibility.
If, therefore, you have on the one hand somewhat of a lessening of the authority of area commanders with respect to the militia by virtue of the fact that a militia directorate has been established, I should think they would tend to say, well, if part of our authority has been taken away, then it is not as in gent that we deal with these matters as it might be if we were directly responsible. Having set up a directorate, I wonder whether it would not be sound to give it a somewhat more direct responsibility in the chain of command between the directorate and the militia units.
I am not blaming the minister because it is probably my fault, but I do not have a very clear picture yet how this thing works. However, as I understand it, it seems to me there is some danger that the militia, rather than assuming a more important place and having a greater degree of priority and urgency attached to their problems, will tend to assume a rather less important place. I would think that could be offset by giving the directorate more and greater authority to issue instructions, make decisions and have them carried out directly in the militia units concerned.

I think the opposite has proven to be the result of the new set-up. Major General Letson, as adviser to the chief fMr. Fulton.]

of the general staff, visits many units, as does Colonel Buell. General Letson also attends all the corps association meetings. In other words, while the channel of official communication is followed

after all, it is one army

the fact that General Letson is special adviser to the chief of the general staff with respect to the militia and Colonel Buell is the director of militia means that they keep in close contact with the militia units, visit them singly or together, and learn at first hand their needs and problems.
Of course General Letson has direct access to the chief of the general staff, and so far as we can tell all phases of the new set-up appear to be working out far more satisfactorily than under the former organization. We also believe it will improve as an understanding of the purpose behind the reorganization wh'ch took place last year becomes more general.

As far as direct contact is concerned, that depends on the ability of General Letson and Colonel Buell to get about the country and make personal visits. Am I not correct in understanding that apart from that there is no direct contact and that these matters go through area and command headquarters? Therefore unless these officers are on tour all the time there is no direct contact.

I think most of the complaints crop up at the corps association meetings which General Letson attends. The members are very frank and outspoken, and I think these meetings are helpful to him because representatives come from all parts of the country. Each corps meets by itself, in addition to the meeting of the conference of defence associations which takes place annually. At these meetings they thresh out all their problems in his presence and his guidance and assistance is available if they require it. I think on the whole the new arrangement has worked out reasonably well.

Mr. Chairman, I was very interested in the discussion carried on the last time the committee examined these estimates with regard to the function of anti-aircraft batteries. The minister indicated the number still in existence in the militia, and I think the implication was that quite a number had been disbanded. I do not think he gave that figure.
In my own riding we had two very old batteries of field artillery that had very proud records as militia units in peacetime and in both world wars. After world war II they were reorganized into a light anti-aircraft unit, and last year that unit was completely disbanded. I have no special complaint to make if the action was unavoidable. I know

that the men who have taken such a keen interest in these militia units for many years will accept that action like the good soldiers they are if it is absolutely essential.
My question is this. I would ask the minister to indicate to the committee what form of organization is taking over the function formerly performed by these light anti-aircraft batteries? I realize, of course, that modern aircraft fly above the effective height of light ack-ack; nevertheless there are many types of conventional warfare in which there is a necessity for light ack-ack to prevent low level attacks on troop concentrations, airfields or special installations. There may be low-flying aircraft which would be armed with anti-personnel bombs, rockets, land mines or something of that sort. I am wondering what has resulted from this reorganization, in the way of means of protecting troops and installations against low-flying aircraft.
I do not pretend to be any expert on armed forces, but I can visualize a situation in which it would be necessary to protect northern airfields and many other installations of that sort against low-level, sneak attacks by enemy aircraft.

The question of anti-aircraft, as the hon. member knows, is one that has gone through a good deal of transition in the last few years. The usefulness of antiaircraft guns for many of the purposes for which they were formerly effective has declined. In our reorganization of the anti-aircraft section of the artillery we have retained 8, I believe, light ack-ack units and 9 heavy units which it is felt, having in mind that most anti-aircraft work is now sought to be performed by aeroplanes, rockets, etc., will be sufficient to take care of those areas where low-flying planes might be expected. Those areas are shrinking. We do not now expect nearly as many low-flying aeroplanes, if an attack were launched, as they would expect to have in Europe, for example. This is because of the distances from base and various other factors.
While we are working on air defences against planes, we are still retaining a certain amount of anti-aircraft, both light and heavy, to cover the situation so far as we think desirable. There may be a further reduction in the number of anti-aircraft units. In England, I believe they have almost eliminated anti-aircraft artillery. The situation is in a state of flux and will have to work itself out as we learn more, as we develop more modern equipment and as we are able to provide new methods to meet the situation.

It would seem now that although the situation is in a state of flux and
Supply-National Defence these units might not for the moment fill a useful purpose, when the situation is further stabilized by developments it may be found that there would be a useful role for these anti-aircraft units if they were equipped with suitable weapons. I refer, of course, to ground to air rockets for defence against high-flying aircraft and also to the manning of radar equipment which might control these rockets after being launched.
Of course this is a very big subject, and is one upon which there are differing views; but I feel that perhaps we should go very cautiously about disbanding any more of these units. Perhaps it was unwise that we acted with such haste in disbanding the ones we had, because while their usefulness may be decreasing in their present form, it may well be that in the near future we will find ourselves in the position of having to reorganize similar units equipped with more modern weapons.
I just wanted to pass on that suggestion with a word of caution, because in the future I feel our big problem in North America is going to be air defence. Whether that will be chiefly achieved by the air force, and air to air defence, or whether there will be an important role for ground to air defence has not been Anally decided, but it seems to me the day may come when it will be well for us to have our chief industrial areas ringed by ground defences equipped with modern rockets to protect the area against high-flying aircraft.

I note that the sum for pay and allowances this year is $10 million. It was the same last year, and if my memory serves me correctly it was the same the year before. Would the minister tell us how much was actually expended for pay and allowances last year?
The amount actually spent last year was $11,000,004.

I wonder if the minister could tell us whether the fact that only $10 million is to be appropriated this year, while $11 million was spent last year, is due to the fact it is expected there will be fewer people in the militia this year going to camp, and so on?

As a matter of fact the number of people who have gone or will go to camp this year is substantially higher than last year. I think a great saving will be effected by the fact that the members of the militia now are pretty well all active members. They are not paid until they serve 15 days. The steps that were taken in connection with the reorganization have resulted

Supply-National Defence in some economies. It is felt that the sum in the estimates this year will be adequate to meet our needs.
I should think there will be fewer people being paid if you are going to pay out less money; is that not the general situation?

Last year, as the hon. member knows, the estimate was $10 million and we spent $11 million. We have budgeted for the same figure because, while we may spend the amount actually spent last year, $11 million, we feel that the savings may be greater this year by reason of economies and better organization. With respect to this matter of the training of the militia and the upkeep of the reserve army, I want to bring to the attention of the minister something of which he has heard before, namely the need for an armoury in my own city. Saskatoon is the home of a regiment which played no mean part in the last war, the Saskatoon Light Infantry. We have a few miles north of our modern and growing city of some 60,000 people a fine air establishment; we have a fine naval establishment, and adjacent to our city we have the military camp of Dundurn.
The missing link is an armoury for Saskatoon. It is a disgrace, I was going to say to the city but I shall change that and say it is a disgrace to the Department of National Defence. If that department wish to encourage the recruitment of young men I would suggest that they give these young men a place in which to train of which they may be proud rather than a place, under present conditions, of which they are ashamed. The temporary quarters have been there for years. It is a hodge-podge business in that there can be no order, and we need an armoury.
I remember four or five years ago, I am not sure of the date, introducing to a Saskatoon audience, I believe it was the Canadian Club, the former minister of national defence, Mr. Claxton. On that occasion he gave us 
what we at least considered to be a commitment of some priority in regard to an armoury for Saskatoon. I told him at that time, jokingly but also seriously, that he would be hearing from me in regard to that commitment in future years. Well, he did hear from me, but up to the present he and his successor have had deaf ears. I know that the mayor of our city has taken up the matter; I know that he is somewhere in the east now with the avowed intention of tracking down the present Minister of National Defence to see if he can use any persuasive powers upon him.
I might point out that our neighbouring and rival city of Regina has a good armoury. We do not like to be second string, and we know we should have an armoury too. As I say, the present accommodation there is really disgraceful. I have been down there on some occasions. I do not know how the men work there or how they train there at all. The minister was expected in Saskatoon the other day, as he probably knows, and we are very disappointed indeed that he did not arrive. We had prepared to meet him.

The hon. member can
attribute that to the present consideration of the estimates.

I know there were circumstances that made it difficult for the minister to be there, and we forgive him for that. We hope he will come at some future date. I happened to be home in connection with the pioneer celebration of the fiftieth anniversary of the official birthday of our province, and we were ready for him; we were going to greet him at the airport. I can assure him that if he had come there he would not only have received a warm welcome but would have received some warm representations as to Saskatoon's need for an armoury.
Our town is proud of her men. They are proud of the part they played in the last war; they are proud of the home regiment, the Saskatoon Light Infantry, to which some reference was made in the debate here yesterday. I am making this further appeal to the minister that something should be done in that regard.
I could talk on this subject at some length, certainly at greater length than I have; but once more I am making this appeal to the minister on behalf of our armed forces in that city, on behalf of the mayor and the city council, and on behalf of the whole population of Saskatoon, whom I am proud to call my constituents. That is all I can do about it. The matter is in the minister's hands. I hope he is prepared to give us some assurance that we shall be well up on the priority

list. I understand that the minister made some reference to priority of armouries this afternoon. I should certainly like to know that Saskatoon is high on that priority list.

speechtext: Northwest highway system.

This item covers the maintenance and operation of the northwest highway system or the Alaska highway as it is commonly known. During the last month or six weeks I have seen a number of newspaper articles and reports to the effect that the Alaska highway was in very bad shape, that it was full of holes and I believe one report indicated that two bridges were out. I have seen a number of warnings to people telling them not to attempt to travel over the Alaska highway. These reports may have been exaggerated, but I should like the minister to tell us the situation as far as the Alaska highway is concerned, what is the condition of the surface of the highway and its general maintenance? Are there any breaks, or are there any bridges out?

As the hon. member knows, the army took over the caretaking, maintenance and operation of the Alaska highway some years ago. Since that time we have been maintaining the highway, doing some


improving of the road and replacing a considerable number of the bridges with permanent structures. I have not been over the Alaska highway, but in the last few months we have received a considerable number of letters commenting favourably on the condition of the highway. One gentleman who drove over it last year was very complimentary regarding the way it is maintained. It is operated of course by the army engineers.
We try to keep the Alaska highway up to a reasonable standard. As far as I know, the people of the locality appear to be satisfied with the condition in which it is maintained. I am not in a position to say how long we shall be in charge of the highway or what its ultimate disposition will be, but since world war II we have been continuously entrusted on behalf of the government with its maintenance.

I have been aware of the fact that, as the minister said, the army has been in control of this highway for a number of years. As a matter of fact it was a very good highway for a considerable length of time, but my questions were directed to the present condition of the highway and whether there are actual breaks in it, owing to bridges being out, etc. In addition to warnings that appeared in Alberta newspapers, I saw a United States newspaper with a fairly big announcement warning people not to go through Canada over the Alaska highway because of the fact that the bridges were out and because of the general condition of the road.

As the hon. member knows, the spring freshets and storms of that area often put the highway out of condition for short periods of time. We keep patrolling the highway, and as soon as any washout or settling of the highway is detected we attempt to put that section into condition as quickly as we can. I have not heard in the last few weeks of any part of the highway not being serviceable. That does not mean some bridge might not have been out. We try to bring it back into use as fast as we can.

I know it is very difficult terrain, and in the spring of the year you are bound to have floods which take out sections of the highway and possibly bridges and so forth. I was hoping the minister could perhaps assure us that by this time those bridges which were apparently out at one time had been replaced, and that the highway was now open and reasonably good for traffic. I think it is a bad thing that there should be a fair amount of publicity because the highway is not fit to be travelled over, or

there are breaks in it so one cannot get through, and that sort of thing.
There is one other question I would like to ask in connection with this. What percentage of this total vote of $2 million-odd, as I recall it, is for maintenance and what percentage is for rebuilding this highway?

I am sorry I have not a breakdown in that way, but I understand nearly the whole of the amount shown in that item is for maintenance of the highway, including bridges. The only item of capital expenditure in the details of the estimates, I believe, is the procurement of equipment, three-quarters of a million dollars. The rest of the charges have to do with the necessary staff and expenditures for maintaining the highway.

I should like to make it plain that nothing I may have said about the highway was critical of the minister or his department as far as this highway is concerned. It runs through country in which it is difficult to keep a highway in good shape. The reason I asked what part of this vote was for rebuilding, as compared with the amount for maintenance, was that I hoped a fair amount of rebuilding might have been going on, which I understand, from what the minister has said, is not the case. I think it is absolutely vital that this highway

the only highway in Canada that leads into the reasonably far north, and the only means by which motor traffic can get into the northern part of this country-be kept in good shape, thus making it possible for motor traffic to get up into the Yukon Territory and to some extent toward the Mackenzie river territory, though there is only one road leading off there, which happens to be in Alberta.
The only way we can expect to have any sort of road system in the north by which wheeled traffic can get into a fair part of the northern territories is to keep this road in good shape. It is the artery by means of which all wheeled traffic gets into a position where it can go into the areas not now served by roads, but which we hope will be so served in the future. As a result I would hope there might be a fair amount of rebuilding done on this highway so it would be kept in good shape. The highway was built during the last war as a military highway. If a certain amount

in fact, a fair amount-is not done to maintain that highway, it is not going to continue to exist and be able to take heavy traffic.

What I call maintenance involves some items which would be really
Supply-National Defence in a sense capital, such as rebuilding of bridges. The report on the highway for last year says:
During the past year army engineers began or completed construction of 13 new steel or concrete bridges replacing temporary wooden bridges erected when the highway was originally pushed through the northern wilderness in 1943 . . . Bridges and some of the 7,000-odd culverts are replaced as the original temporary structures become uneconomical or hazardous.
The item for maintenance probably includes some amounts for straightening sections of the highway and there is a considerable sum for bridges and culverts. We are trying to maintain a good standard on the highway, and that accounts for the fact that the maintenance costs are rather high. The work involves replacement as well as ordinary maintenance.

I am very glad to hear that probably a fair proportion of this vote is for what I should think is essential rebuilding, and that permanent bridges, culverts, and so forth are going into this highway. I would hope that this program might be continued, and also that some start might be made on surfacing that road.

I just want to ask a couple of questions here, Mr. Chairman. There is over $11 million spent on this road. As the hon. member who just sat down has pointed out, I believe part of this road should be gradually hard-surfaced. I think a hard permanent surface should be put in there. I notice that there are a few new positions shown here. There is a matron, who is new this year. There is a plumber supervisor, who is new this year. There are also two upholsterers. What do they do? Do they upholster seats for the men on the highway or what?

We have a good many camps and a good many permanent married quarters for the staff which operates the highway. All these properties must be maintained. Offhand I cannot give the number of married quarters in the various camps we maintain, but they are substantial in number. The furniture, the plumbing and the equipment of these quarters must be maintained, just as the highway must be maintained. Unless you have people in that part of the country who can do such maintenance along that highway, it is rather difficult to get them done because much of the highway is in a remote part of the country. The highway is between 1,200 and 1,300 miles long, so its maintenance is quite a large operation.

Then you have in the estimates this year cement finishers, who were not in the estimates last year. They are for those bridges, are they?

Let him provide people who can give technical assistance and do the necessary work to improve the highway where it should be improved, and not start with an additional group of clerks and typists.
