speechtext: Shall we pass on to the next item, Northwest Territories and Yukon radio system? I take it that is carried. We come now to the Royal Canadian Air Force, regular and general.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think I will be regarded as speaking from a prejudiced point of view if I suggest at the opening of my remarks that in giving consideration to the Royal Canadan Air Force we are dealing with a very important part of the Canadian defence organization, if not the most important part of our defence system. In the white paper on defence tabled in the house there is a very interesting paragraph on page 4 in which the minister recognizes the increasing importance of the air force in the defence role today. In paragraph 7 he says:
For North America, the possibility appears for the first time of an attack that could cripple the military and industrial potential of Canada and the United States. Should we ever be attacked with thermonuclear weapons, it is plain that our immediate problem would be national survival.
The minister has said that for the first time in our history it appears that an attack could cripple the military and industrial potential of Canada. I do not quite agree that this is the first time such an eventuality has become evident. Since the end of world war II voices have been raised from time to time suggesting that in the event of another outbreak of hostilities in this new atomic era, the fate of mankind as a whole would be weighed in the balance.
Over the week end we have had this viewpoint underscored by the statement issued by Lord Bertrand Russell on behalf of nine eminent world scientists. Their statement has again indicated the tremendous danger confronting us in this hydrogen bomb age. I, of course, along with every other member who speaks on this subject, express the hope that the sheer horror of it all will increase the chances for world peace, and there are hopeful signs that this may be the case as we note with considerable relief the apparent easing of world tensions today.
However, we must not refuse to face realities, confronted as we are by these threats; nor should we become mesmerized like the rabbit into a state of paralysis. We have to face the grim possibilities of the situation, and I think it is an encouraging sign when we note the swing of opinion in the country toward the importance of air power in the face of this most threatening danger.
Canada's air defence program has been moving forward with increasing speed since the Korean crisis. There was considerable crash planning evident when we were faced
6026	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence with the crisis of 1950 and 1951, and that crash planning resulted in some criticisms from this side of the house when the defence estimates were before us. I think, however, we have now progressed in the equipping of the R.C.A.F. to such an extent that there is room for a considerable degree of satisfaction, and that we are at least in a position to put up a creditable defence should an attack come from over our northern waste lands.
I am pleased to note that the new minister, whenever he has the opportunity of speaking on this subject, is more inclined to take the people of Canada into his confidence, and I noted that in several of his public statements he has been very frank in expressing the problem and trying to awaken Canadians to their individual responsibility in these matters. There has also been a very healthy shift in greater emphasis toward the problems of home defence, and it is in this area that I believe the R.C.A.F. has the greatest role to play. In defending ourselves against any possible hydrogen bomb attack we are almost completely dependent in the initial stages at least upon the air defence powers that are at our disposal.
The first arm of that defence program is, of course, radar; and we seem to be progressing toward the successful completion of a comprehensive program in that regard. I sometimes wonder whether the public are not labouring under a misapprehension that once we have the three radar defence lines in place and operating across the broad expanse of our country everything will be under control so far as our defence needs are concerned. Obviously that is just the beginning because radar, after all, is merely a warning device established to give the air power at our command sufficient warning to cope with any possible threat. Actually the radar defence is merely a beginning.
I think we should note in this regard that it is most imperative, in view of the threat of thermonuclear war, that warning be given at the earliest possible moment, because if we delay interception until the attacking bombers arrive over the built-up areas it would not be too pleasant an experience to have those attacking forces shot down in the midst of our cities, particularly when they are carrying hydrogen bombs. We have had broad hints that the D.E.W. line, the distant early warning program, is well under way, and that is encouraging indeed.
The chief arm in our defence is a Canadian-built aircraft equipped with a Canadian jet engine, the Orenda. We are informed in the white paper that there will be nine permanent squadrons fully equipped with CF-100 allweather jet fighters. The statement that they 

will be so equipped at the end of the year I think stretches the point somewhat, because in my own mind I have tried to count up the number of active squadrons already equipped, and I cannot get beyond four. But at least it is a consummation devoutly to be wished. I think even when we do have nine squadrons equipped with CF-lOO's we are hardly in a position to defend Canada across the entire length of the country.
There were some questions raised in the house concerning the effectiveness of the CF-100 when the scheme was first contemplated, and when it was under way. According to reports that aircraft has fully justified itself. Experts inform us that it is among the best of the front-line fighter aircraft in operation at the present time. I would imagine that is largely due to the Orenda engine rather than any radical change in the basic design of the aircraft, because as you look at the CF-100 it seems to be a largely conventional aircraft from the aerodynamics standpoint, tied in with a very powerful jet engine. However, there is reasonable assurance that the CF-100 will serve Canada for at least the next four or five years.
In view of these circumstances I have been somewhat surprised to find, judging from newspaper reports-there has been no formal statement in the house to this effect-that there has been a cut-back in the rate of production of the CF-100. There have been lay-offs at the A. V. Roe plant at Malton. I find this difficult to understand, in view of the necessity of equipping at least six additional active squadrons with this type of aircraft, and also in view of the continuing demands from other sources that have been hinted at as a result of the demonstrated effectiveness of this aircraft. There has also been a $100 million cut in expenditures for the procurement of aircraft and engines. I have been checking through the discussion to date, Mr. Chairman, and I have looked into all published documents very carefully, but I have not seen any explanation that would cover this particular situation.
Have we enough planes to meet our growing commitments, both at home and abroad?
I hardly believe the information we have before us at the moment indicates that such is the case. Rather I would imagine the A. V. Roe company should be operating at maximum capacity in order to meet the very urgent demands to deal with the situation that is frankly acknowledged in the white paper, and frankly acknowledged by all those who have responsibility for these matters. It seems to me that a situation of this kind suggests a degree of uncertainty, if not confusion, as we are approaching the demands

of a new era in defensive measures as a result of the potential threat of thermonuclear warfare.
I have not been able to get too much information either, Mr. Chairman, on the armament situation. Armament, of course, is basic to aircraft. Just as the aircraft has to fit into the radar scheme of things, in the final analysis a fighter plane really is merely an airborne armament platform. I realize there are matters of security involved. We have very broad generalizations concerning the use of guided missiles, air to air guided missiles and ground to air guided missiles, but we do not have too much specific information as to just how far advanced we are in this program of providing the new type of armament to deal with a new kind of threat from the air. I am amazed to discover, for example, we are still producing large quantities of 50-calibre ammunition, which was used in the traditional Browning type of machine gun which actually was obsolete at the end of world war II.
I know there are air to air rockets available now on our defensive fighters, but then again it would seem to me their effectiveness would be limited by the aerodynamic problems they create, particularly when they are slung outside high speed aircraft. These are matters concerning which perhaps it is impossible to give too much specific information, but nonetheless they are very important if we are going to prepare ourselves adequately to meet any possible threat from the air.
It occurred to me that one of the reasons for the cut-back in the production of the CF-100 arises from the change in plans for our auxiliary squadrons. There are 10 auxiliary squadrons in Canada that have been making a very effective contribution under very difficult circumstances during recent years as a result of lack of modern equipment and facilities of that kind. Last year in the white paper it was intimated that these auxiliary squadrons would be converted to CF-100 all-weather fighters. We raised a query at the time as to the feasibility of this program, in view of the very complex nature of the CF-100 flying operation, particularly the radar part of their equipment. I note that it has now been decided not to go forward with this plan for the auxiliary squadrons, and perhaps herein lies the reason for the cut-back in CF-100 production. It could be that the chief demand for additional CF-lOO's arose from the plans to equip our auxiliary squadrons with that type of aircraft.
That immediately raises the query as to what is to be done with our auxiliary squadrons. There are vague indications that 50433-381J
Supply-National Defence they could be used for transport work, for coastal command work, and certainly they could fit into that scheme of things and make an excellent contribution. However, Mr;>
Chairman, several speakers from this side of the house have suggested the necessity for providing a mobile striking force that would be largely along the lines of an airborne force. It seems to me that if such a force were contemplated our auxiliary squadron personnel could fit in very nicely here.
I believe that Canadair is going to manufacture or is in the process of manufacturing the Bristol Britannia turbojet. This type of aircraft produced under licence in a Canadian factory would be an excellent successor to the North Star, which has served its time and is now passing into obsolescence along with other conventional aircraft. The Bristol Britannia, or some similar aircraft, might provide just the type of machine that is needed to equip the auxiliary squadrons in order to provide this mobile, airborne striking force.
It occurs to me, for example, that in addition to providing incentive for auxiliary squadron personnel it would help provide incentive for army personnel by stimulating their interest in laying on trans-Atlantic operations. If we had the equipment, aircraft of the turbojet type, certainly the problems of distance would be reduced to such an extent that we could operate on an intercontinental basis, thereby cutting down the necessity of maintaining a large standing force of Canadian army personnel on the continent.
The main justification for that situation has been that it is a morale booster for people on the continent to see Canadian army personnel actually in their midst. I am sure that if we had a mobile airborne striking force engaged in intercontinental exercises this would have the same effect of maintaining the morale of our European NATO allies.
This is merely one thought that comes to my mind. On the other hand there are the deficiencies in our tactical air command group that I feel should be taken into consideration. We actually have a tactical air command in the R.C.A.F. at the moment, but it seems to me that it has been a very sadly neglected part of our air force operation. So far as I can gather it consists of two Mitchell squadrons, and the dear old Mitchell aircraft was obsolete in world war II. Last year we discussed this to a limited extent, and at page 6435 of Hansard the former minister of national defence had this to say regarding Mitchells:
Mitchells are going to continue to be used for the operation of cleaning up any landings that might take place. They are very good aircraft for the purpose.
6028	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence In the year that has passed since that statement was made, and in view of the new emphasis indicated in the white paper, that jsoint of view no longer holds true in defence quarters. No doubt the officials are very rapidly coming to the conclusion that our two obsolete Mitchell squadrons are not too effective in dealing with the responsibilities that would fall to a tactical air command air force in the event of hostilities.
I believe tactical air command provides for a versatility, assuming that you had the right aircraft, that would make it possible for such a group to operate in several areas of our air defence program. I am thinking now in terms of the versatility of the famous Mosquito of world war II. In those days the Mosquito served in almost every possible capacity in the air war, and did it very effectively indeed. There seems to be no reason why a similar jet type aircraft of the same versatile qualities could not be developed and supplied as equipment for tactical air command.
If our 10 auxiliary squadrons, which are apparently at the moment foot-loose and fancy free, were equipped with that type of aircraft they might operate, for example, under tactical air command, doubling as day fighters if the all-weather fighter proposition provides complexities too great for a parttime flyer to overcome. It is quite feasible that the auxiliary aircrew could cope effectively as day fighters and perform the basic function of ground support for troops against airborne attacks that might be aimed at our distant early warning radar units. No doubt the first objective of any potential enemy would be to destroy the effectiveness of our radar installations, and there is where a tactical air force would come in very handy indeed. Also, we have no bomber force, and there are no possibilities in Canada of moving into that aerial activity, mainly because our chief responsibility in the scheme of continental defence is defensive. But a versatile aircraft might easily be used as a low-level bomber, particularly for the pin-point type of bombing that was done so efficiently by the Mosquito during the last world war.
I have not sufficient technical knowledge to know whether our own CF-100 is a suitably versatile aircraft in this regard. If it is as efficient as the experts indicate, if it is as effective and as flexible as newspaper stories indicate, it seems to me quite logical to conclude that our own all-Canadian CF-100 might be such an aircraft.
Last year we were contemplating equipping our auxiliary squadrons with the all-weather fighter. That has not been found impossible, 

but still it might be possible to equip auxiliary squadrons with the day type of fighter to minimize all the complicated radar paraphernalia and the other electronic equipment that is necessary in this type of aircraft. These are some suggestions that have come to my mind, with my limited background, because of problems of security and so forth, as I have tried to give some thought to this matter.
The air force, or any part of the armed forces, is not worth very much unless we have the manpower to back it up. I want to speak just briefly on that problem, and in this connection I would refer to a question answered on May 2 of this year. Apparently the problem of obtaining suitable aircrew is assuming almost insurmountable proportions, and the hon. member for York West asked a series of questions dealing with this subject. The return brought down indicated that in 1954 out of a total of some 5,570 applications for enlistment as aircrew there were over 4,000 rejections. Those rejections were divided into three categories. Physical disability accounted for 312; failure to meet educational standard, 80; and other reasons, 3,729. I do not know what the other reasons would be, but the largest group fell into that category. That indicates a great wastage among applicants for aircrew, and no doubt for those who are in touch with the problem it presents a difficult situation.
Obviously the operation of modern jet and supersonic aircraft requires the best of personnel. This was so in world war II, when the selection was carefully carried out. However, it seems to me that we should be able to get a better proportion than was indicated by this return of May 2. I do not know whether it is that the right type of young Canadian is not offering himself for service, or whether the desire to fly the vast uncharted sanctity of space which drew so many into the air force in world war II is no longer present. Perhaps the minister could touch on this matter when he replies to some of these observations.
No doubt the crash record in the air force has been somewhat of a deterrent. I raise this issue not as a cause of further discouragement to anyone who might be interested in an air force career, but rather to point out what was indicated in a return tabled on May 18 in reply to questions concerning T-33 crashes in Canada since this aircraft was put into service. The return indicates that there have been 39 crashes, of which 30 were in training command. In reply to the question as to the principal reason for crashes it was stated to be error in judgment

on the part of the pilot. In other words it was not a structural or mechanical failure; it was an error on the part of the pilot in control of the aircraft.
To me that is a most significant answer, as it suggests that there may be something wrong in the training program. From time to time we on this side have indicated a growing concern over the substitution of a two-stage training program for the three-stage program which operated so successfully in world war II. Somewhere in the white paper it is stated that an order for 60 Chipmunk aircraft had been placed with the de Havilland aircraft company, which would indicate that we are going to use the Chipmunk as a basic trainer. No doubt this plan has been motivated by the fact that there have been such a large number of accidents in training command resulting from error in judgment on the part of the pilot.
We had sufficient experience with the commonwealth air training plan during world war II to realize that sound fundamental basic training is absolutely essential for the success of a military pilot. I am informed that was one of the fatal errors made by the luftwaffe. It attempted to streamline its training in order to get operational pilots into service more quickly, with rather devastating results to its efficiency. I am sure if there has been any deterrent to the enlistment of young Canadians of the right kind who can meet the physical, mental and other requirements, the knowledge that the Chipmunk is to be used as a basic trainer will tend to remove such deterrent.
There is another matter which comes to my mind. I am informed that the risk pay for members of the R.C.A.F. at the present time is something like $30 per month. As I recall, that is not as good as the risk pay the aircrew received during world war II. I have checked into the figures for the United States air force, and find that the risk pay there amounts to something like $170 a month. It is hard to say what a suitable relationship for the R.C.A.F. would be, but I imagine that on a comparative basis it should be something like $75 a month. In view of the demands created by the flying of high-speed modern jet military aircraft, an incentive of this kind would be of some importance in interesting our young Canadians in entering upon a flying career with the R.C.A.F.
So much for the permanent force. There are other things that could be mentioned, but we have not the necessary time. I should like to refer briefly to the reserve. As with the army, the R.C.A.F. reserve is the backbone of any wartime air force. In view of
Supply-National Defence the changed status of the reserve and the role it is to play in the new emphasis on air power, I think there is a great opportunity to create renewed interest in the R.C.A.F. reserve program. If the auxiliary squadrons can be converted to a challenging and responsible role, I have no doubt at all that Canadians will respond accordingly to the opportunities provided.
I should like to say just one word on the very excellent mobilization assignment training program that is making effective use of veterans of world war II. I believe the scheme has been meeting with increasing success, particularly since it has been made available to senior N.C.O's. One comment has come my way from those who have participated in this scheme. As the minister knows, this is a program whereby a member of the reserve air force understudies some particular permanent force position. I know of one instance, for example, where a flight lieutenant is understudying a wing commander, and he has turned out for four successive summers now. His civilian role is that of managing a very large and active automobile business, and he is himself a qualified engineer. Yet when he turns out for his annual period of training with the M.A.T.P. he has no other incentive but his desire to serve some useful purpose in our defence program. I am wondering whether the incentive of giving a reservist of that kind acting rank equivalent to the position he is understudying might not result in increased interest in this very worth-while activity.
I am informed that my time is almost up, and I shall close with a very brief comment. I do not know whether the minister has any influence at all in regard to the manufacture of military aircraft, but I have on several occasions directed the attention of the Minister of Defence Production to the rather futile approach of concentrating this kind of production in our large urban centres. I have been reading a report on the operations of A. V. Roe, and I notice there has been an attempt to decentralize the operations involved in the manufacture of the Orenda engine to the extent that now over 70 per cent of the Orenda engine is manufactured outside the Malton plant by more than 400 Canadian companies stretching from the maritime provinces to the middle west. In the opening paragraph of his report the defence minister stated:
It is now clear that a single thermonuclear bomb can be made large enough to destroy a major city and all its inhabitants by direct effects of blast and heat.

Supply-National Defence This indicates that the need for dispersal of our essential defence production has become imperative indeed.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two observations on the remarks of the hon. member. First I should like to say that he obviously retains a deep interest in the Royal Canadian Air Force and has followed its development very closely. I should like to take the opportunity to correct a figure in the return to which he referred. It indicated that during 1954 rejections were as follows for aircrew:
(i) physical disability	 312
(ii)	failure to meet educational standard ...	80
(iii) other reasons	 3,729
As a matter of fact the figure of 3,729 included by inadvertence 1,207 people who merely made an inquiry and also 1,393 who made a contact and voluntarily withdrew before being examined for enrolment. The figure should therefore be about 1,200 rejected for other reasons instead of 3,729. I did not want to leave it on the record as it is in Hansard, because it is obviously a rather ridiculous figure.
Another matter to which I wish to refer is the T-33 crashes. We regret these crashes, of course, and it is a matter of concern to the R.C.A.F., but the facts are that our T-33 jet crashes are a little lower than those of the British and just a shade higher than the American. They seem to run in groups, as they do in other countries.
The third matter I should like to mention is that the Chipmunk now being adopted in the training program has no relevance to the T-33 position. It is felt that the training wastage will be substantially reduced if we take first a simpler plane for the purpose of training. It is considered that this will show whether a man has any inherent disabilities and cannot learn to fly and, if that is so, the sooner his training is stopped the better. Second, it introduces him more gradually into flying than going directly on to a Harvard. But there is no relevance between the change-over from two-stage training to three-stage training and the crashes of the T-33 aircraft.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to take the time of the committee to discuss the details of the various portions of the estimates with respect to the air command at this time. However, I should like to stress that I feel we should not minimize the value of our air force at this time, particularly when we are discovering that we are able to negotiate through strength. I am satisfied the minister is recognizing that fact, since
[Mr. Dinsdale.l
he is asking for something like $800 million for our air force expenditures out of a total of $1,729 million.
The matter that bothers me, however, is more particularly contained on page 340 of the estimates. We have on that page for the purchase of real properties, land and buildings, an estimated $3,590,000 for this year as against $1,400,000 for last year. That is an increase of $2,100,000. If we are going to improve our air force and add to it, we are necessarily going to require more land and buildings. However, the construction of buildings and works is a different matter, apparently. We are reducing the estimate from $107 million in 1954-55 to $69,660,000 for this year, or a reduction of approximately $37,340,000.
I think that is a retrograde step. We are reducing our construction of buildings and works for defence purposes in possibly the most important-or certainly one that has been regarded by many as the most important-of the services. That is particularly true in the light of the fact that on the same page we have for repairs and upkeep of buildings and works, including land, an expenditure of $8,243,000, as compared with the estimated $6 million for 1954-55. That is, the increase would be some $2,243,000 for repairs and upkeep of buildings. We are similarly increasing our rentals of lands and buildings to $2,228,000 this year from $1,406,000 last year. As we note from these figures, or as a study of them will indicate, apparently we are going to build less but are going to rent more. That might be taken to mean that the government are looking hard to see whether they cannot find people who are willing to construct buildings for them to use. We are not cutting down on our air expenses to the extent that we do not require more buildings. We apparently do require more, because we are going to spend more on rents. Therefore we are going to make it possible for people to build these buildings for us and for us to rent them from them, and thereby possibly gain more political heelers.
Those charges can be made and are being made. I refer specifically to a Vancouver Sun article of Monday, July 4. The title of it is "City Battles Ramp Claim". I am not so much interested in the struggle between the city and this particular company, but part of the article reads as follows:
The one-storey building, 1367 Howe, rented by the air force's ground observer corps, is claimed by its owners to have dropped $35,000 in value . . .
Owners are R. Rowe Holland and William Couper.

I personally do not know either of these men, so I cannot speak as to their political affiliations. However, here is what the article says:
He-
That is Mr. Holland.
-and Mr. Couper built at a cost of $42,296, Mr. Holland testified.
Value of the two lots on which the building is located was said by Mr. Holland to be $15,000 in 1952.
In other words we have here a total expenditure of something over $57,000. Now the rental on that building, according to the article, is $750 per month. The over-all receipts that Couper and Holland will receive from this building will be something over $58,000 in a period of seven years. The lease terminates apparently in 1959.
The question is this. Is it good business for the government to rent a building that costs- that is taking into consideration the over-all cost of the land or property, building, etc.- something like $57,000 and then pay rent of just over $58,000 for the use of that building for a period of seven years?
Ordinarily business property in the area may rent at that particular figure. But whether or not it is a good investment from a governmental point of view is entirely a different question. Business personnel, in leasing such a piece of property, do so with another purpose in mind entirely. They choose a site on which they want their particular business house placed, and they usually choose it with a view of customer attraction and with other factors taken into consideration, such as parking, etc.
Apparently those factors are not necessarily taken into consideration when the government asks other individuals to build a building on a particular location for them. The fact remains, however, that in the case of business the matter that is important is to have customer appeal because they intend to make a profit from that particular venture. So the business house, generally speaking, constructs its own building. Then it turns around and sells that business block to another individual who will become the landlord. They may even arrange in the lease to repay him in that seven-year period the value of the property. That is, the amount of the lease might amount to that sum.
However, business has the use of the capital they have invested in that building originally to make a profit therefrom in a general turnover of the stock; thereby it would cut back the rent considerably from what the government is forced to pay. We do not rent these buildings on the same basis that business is renting them. We do not expect to
Supply-National Defence make a profit out of the air force offices. At least, if we do so, I have not heard of any. I would say that it is most important to examine into this situation. I cannot blame the men who have been asked to build these blocks for the government for the purpose for which they might do it. I cannot blame the present Minister of National Defence. He was not here as minister in 1952 in charge of this department-or was he?
No.

No, he was not. However, I would say that at the time of leasing the building these factors should have been taken into consideration. If the government ask an individual to build a building for them, no matter who the individual is and no matter what party affiliations he might have, I personally would feel that he is not to blame. I cannot see that we could attach any particular blame to him. However, it is a mistake on the part of government to invest, on a rental basis, funds which would in themselves repay the cost of building that building in a short period of time such as seven years.
I would ask that the minister examine into these factors. I would ask that he possibly set up a committee to examine into the rentals of these various buildings. We have, for instance, editorials along these particular lines. The Vancouver Sun carried one. The British Columbian of New Westminster of Thursday, July 7, had this to say in an editorial entitled "Check Rein on Rentals". I may say that it is referring to governmental buildings, but others are referred to as well:
The rents paid here, it seems, are no higher than the government pays in other parts of the nation, and while some may he exorbitant, most premises bring from the federal government about the same as the owners could get from private businesses.
I suggested that was a possibility, as you will recall. The article goes on further to say this:
The government should, too, show the basis it employs for setting the rate of rental it will pay, and if these are so high as to encourage political manoeuvres, they should be revised.
Mr. Chairman, I am satisfied that any individual, no matter who he might be, would have little difficulty in arranging the finances to build such a building if he could go to a financier and say, "I have a contract with the dominion government guaranteeing a seven-year lease and in the period of the seven-year lease the building will be paid for." That in itself is an exorbitant rate of rent. The lease is too high. It should be examined into. The fact that business-and "business" is not governmental business but private enterprise-would be willing to invest in a
6032	HOUSE OF
Supply-National Defence lease of that type does not necessarily exonerate our government or any other government from responsibility for such a reactionary method as that in which it follows in renting its buildings.
The fact remains that if the individual can rent the building to the government or can get from the government a lease by whose terms the building would be paid for in a matter of seven years or less, then I would say the government should be called upon to build such a building on its own, and we could well save the taxpayers millions of dollars by so doing. That is one reason I take exception. to the fact that instead of investing $107 million as we had proposed in 1954 and 1955, this year we should anticipate expenditures of only $69,660,000 in comparison. We are cutting our building expenditures there, as I said earlier, by something like $27 million while at the same time we are going to increase the expenditure for rentals. I am satisfied, Mr. Chairman, that if we are going to increase our rentals across the nation it means only one thing. It means that the more people who are interested in leasing buildings to the government, the more people there will be who are going to turn into government supporters by reason of the fact that they have a contract with the government to lease a building to them. That in itself is wrong.

Perhaps I might be permitted to refer briefly to the four items on page 340 to which the hon. member referred. The first has to do with rentals of land, buildings and works. The figure in the estimates last year, as he mentioned, was $1,406,000, and this year the figure is $2,228,000. The major part of that increase is entirely due to the rental agreements with the French and German governments with respect to married quarters, schools and other buildings which were occupied during the year for the first time. Therefore the increase is attributable almost entirely to our overseas rentals.
Then the hon. member mentioned the item having to do with repairs and upkeep of buildings and works, and made reference to the fact that last year the estimate was $6 million and this year it is $8,243,000. I am informed that the actual expenditure during the fiscal year 1954-55 wgs not $6 million but $8,900,000. The item was underestimated, and the actual figure was $700,000 greater than the estimate for this year.
With respect to the item having to do with the construction of buildings and works, the estimate for 1954-55 was $107 million and the estimate this year is $69,660,000. I am informed that of the estimated expenditure of


$107 million for last year under that head, only $59 million was actually spent. This year we are counting on spending $69 million so the figure is up rather than down, assuming that we spend what we have estimated this year.
The fourth item to which the hon. member referred has to do with the purchase of real properties. The figure this year is $3,590,000 compared with $1,400,000 last year. The increase is almost entirely due to purchases and settlements in the Primrose lake and Cold lake areas where we have the guided missile weapons range. Therefore the figures in the estimates probably do not quite reflect the actual conditions as they are.

I appreciate the straightforward way in which the minister has answered some of my questions, but there is one factor remaining in connection with the rental of buildings. What is the policy of the Department of National Defence with respect to the rental of buildings? Is it expected that the lessor should have his building paid for in a matter of seven years? Would the minister outline to us just how they go about leasing a building?

With respect to our rental of buildings, we act almost entirely through the Department of Public Works. I understand there are appraisers who fix the values. They proceed on a pattern of determining the value of the building and fixing a reasonable rental. I am not familiar with the matter to which the hon. member refers, but on the other hand I would think that the return of the capital cost of a building in seven years might be out of line.

Along that line I am going to suggest to the minister that possibly he should take it upon himself, if he considers such a return to be out of line, to discuss the matter with his colleagues in the hope of possibly instituting an impartial inquiry into all rentals of this type. I am very pleased to hear his statement because it bears out what I have been told by private appraisers with respect to this particular building, in connection with which it is suggested that the rent might have been $550 a month at one time but if it were set at $400 now it would be much more in line.

Mr. Chairman, for several days I and the minister's air advisers have sat in the house with a fairly good display of patience, I think, and have heard the house discuss alternatively reform of the Senate and the army estimates. I hope this was just a coincidence and that there is no special

significance to the close sequence of the discussion of these two topics.
I think probably the most important problem facing us as a nation in the policy field as far as defence is concerned is one of definition. I have the feeling that there is a great deal of uncertainty and woolly thinking about what our position is, what our requirements are and what progress we are making toward meeting those requirements after they have been established. There is a quotation to be found somewhere in the Bible, I think in Corinthians, to the effect that if the trumpets give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to battle? On one occasion Field Marshal Montgomery recommended the reading of that verse to the chiefs of staff. Perhaps something along that line would not be amiss at the present time.
I believe that if our defence effort is to be successful the general public must be convinced of its usefulness. They must be convinced that both their money and the human effort involved are being used to the best possible advantage. Therefore I think we need a clear and certain sound regarding our defence requirements. I realize reasonably well, I think, that in recent years there have been very rapid changes in the concepts of defence because of the rapid advances that have been made in the application of scientific knowledge to the art of war. For that reason I am not in any way trying to belittle the problem that faces those whose responsibility it is to guide our defence effort.
Of course there are certain truisms. We want to be strong as a nation so we can negotiate through strength and deter aggression. But that leads immediately to the problem of where that strength should be deployed and displayed, and how and where we can best deter aggression. I think there should be a very careful reassessment of the role of the three services in our defence effort, a reassessment of what we need in the way of a navy, an army and an air force. It is just possible that the changes in the relative importance of the three services should be further adjusted.
Very important too is the question of defence research. From my point of view I think that is the most vital thing in the long run. After all, our ability to defend ourselves in the near future depends on what research we do now. That research, of course, applies to all three services, but perhaps to the air force more than the others.
A vital subject, too-of course it does not come into this debate and I only refer to it briefly-is that of civil defence. We hear a great number of conflicting statements so far 50433-382
Supply-National Defence as that is concerned. On the one hand people say our civil defence is all it needs to be. On the other hand you hear people say civil defence is hopeless. Then in between you have all the other different points of view. At the moment I want to confine myself chiefly, Mr. Chairman, and I think you will be pleased to hear me say this, to the role of the air force in defence. World war I made two great revolutionary contributions to warfare. One was the tank and the other was the aeroplane. World war II also made two new revolutionary contributions, the atomic bomb and the rocket-propelled missile.
In the light of these developments I am rather concerned about what appears to be a growing complex regarding defensive measures, and a tendency to lull ourselves into a sense of false security in the belief that we can wall ourselves about with a line of some sort through which no aggressor can come. One does not have to go very far back into history to realize that was exactly the thinking that grew up in France after their experience in world war I. They built the Maginot line at terrific expense, and bragged about their security against aggression from any outside source.
I am afraid there is a tendency for us to look with satisfaction at the great amount of money that is required for our various warning lines of defence, the "Pinetree" line, the mid-Canada line, and the D.E.W. line. I am not trying to detract from those lines in any way or from the necessity of erecting them, but I think we should not place undue confidence in them.
In that regard I should like to quote very briefly from a lecture given by Field Marshal Montgomery to the Royal United Services Institute in October of last year. In one place he had this to say:
There is at the present time no sure defence against the aeroplane or ballistic rocket. Indeed, so far as we can see today, trying to get a secure defence against air attack is rather like trying to keep the tide back on the seashore with a picket fence. This situation must not be allowed to continue. The best scientific brains we possess should be gathered in to help in the task, working in close co-operation with air forces. I say "air forces" because I hold the view that air defence should be organized and handled by air forces, and that ack-ack commands should be handed over to that service.
That is the opinion of one who I think could be justly said to be fairly highly qualified to pass an opinion. We should not forget, therefore, that if we hope to deter aggression the only way we can achieve that is to be in a position to retaliate with great force and great speed against any would-be aggressor.

Supply-National Defence In that connection I should like to quote very briefly from an article written by Professor Stanley, professor of history at the Royal Military College. He says in part: More and more one is forced to the conclusion that both of the senior services must yield priority to their junior sister as the major fighting service of the war to come. Soldiers and sailors may still think in terms of "balanced forces'', but such thinking is more wishful than rational. "Massive deterrent air power" is our best hope for keeping the cold war on ice, but there are no dividends to be earned in building conventional forms of aircraft merely because they fly in the air. Fast jet -^bombers and jet interceptors with the latest scientific inventions are required.
There is an even stronger argument, I think, for the need for the ability to retaliate. This brings me to the second great development of world war II, the long-range jet-propelled missile. So far as I know there is no known defence against the type of missile which is related to the V-2 that was used towards the end of world war II. These things render radar lines obsolete. In the last eight months of world war II about 1,050 V-2's were fired on English soil, and about half of them landed in London. During that time Britain's radar defences were at a very high peak of efficiency, yet they succeeded in detecting less than half of these V-2's, and they succeeded in plotting the course of less than one-third of them. Of course conventional aircraft, regardless of their speed, are incapable of intercepting such missiles because even world war II missiles had a speed twice that of sound. In most cases they would arrive before anyone was aware they were coming. During the war there was a saying that if you heard a V-2 it had not hit you, and you were safe.
I notice, Mr. Chairman, it is ten o'clock.
Carry on.

speechtext:
I have not had an opportunity of addressing myself to any of the hon. gentlemen opposite, but would it be possible for us to continue this debate for a while?
I think the debate is going along at a fairly high level, and perhaps we could continue.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed that this debate continue?
Agreed.

I do not want to be accused of taking a compliment at face value, but I may perhaps go on for a while to conclude my remarks. Perhaps then the committee could rise and report progress.
When I was interrupted, Mr. Chairman, I was referring to the fact that really modern projectiles of the V-2 type will, in the very near future, probably make radar defensive warning lines obsolete if they are built and

designed only for the purpose of warning of approaching aircraft. However, it may be possible that some use can be made of them in future by developments which would allow the ground to air missiles to intercept these rockets coming from other areas before they arrive at their target. There may be developments that will allow radar automatically to intercept these missiles coming from outside our borders.
Since I have said that, I think it should be evident that it is highly important, above all else, to keep pace with progress. History teaches us that victors in wars become complacent and satisfied with their achievements, while the losers and the near-losers are whipped into a frenzy of action, and their development is apt to be more rapid than that of the victors. I feel there is a danger that we may fall into complacency in this regard. We do not want to develop a Maginot line complex as far as our radar lines and our conventional air defences are concerned.
This, of course, needs vision and imagination. It requires sound thinkers who can look at the lessons of past military endeavours and learn from them. If you have the odd genius who can have a flash of real imagination and make some revolutionary predictions as to what the future is likely to hold, so much the better. If we had a modern Tennyson he could probably give us a clue or two as to what is really going to happen in the future. After all I think it was in the 1840's, and that was quite a long while ago, when Tennyson wrote some really prophetic lines in "Loeksley Hall." He said, as I remember it:
For I dipt into the future, far as human eye could see,
Saw the Vision of the world, and all the wonder that would be;
Saw the heavens fill with commerce, argosies of magic sails,
Pilots of the purple twilight, dropping down with costly bales;
Heard the heavens fill with shouting, and there rain'd a ghastly dew
From the nations' airy navies grappling in the central blue.
That is a fairly accurate description of the state of affairs in which the world finds itself at the present time. But I do not think we can fairly expect the minister to have geniuses of that calibre on his staff. The least we can demand is that we have men who are capable and are given the opportunity-I think that is even more important-to assess as accurately as possible the very marked development and changes that have taken place at the present time. We must remember that wars are never won by using the methods of previous wars entirely. We must retain, of course, that which was effective

and will prove to be effective in the future, but we must also not be averse to change.
As far as the development of rockets is concerned, it does not take any genius to realize that if the Germans in world war II had a V-2 that could carry an atomic warhead, London would have been written off the map in very short order. The development of rockets has not ceased. As a matter of fact, at the close of world war II the Russians were successful in capturing most of the German experts who were in Peene-munde, and they have no doubt made great advances along that line. Even the V-2, at the end of world war II, was a weapon that had considerable range and, more important still, the Germans at that time had a two-stage rocket in the development stage which would have had a range of 3,000 miles and a speed of about 8,000 miles an hour. That, of course, would be an intercontinental rocket. There is information-I do not know how accurate it is at the present time-that the Russians have succeeded in developing a rocket of this type with a range of about 1,700 miles.
That brings us to the question of where such a thing might be used. At the present time the obvious target for missiles of that sort, especially if they had atomic warheads, would be the large cities of western Europe, such as Paris, London, and so forth. So far as I know there is no conventional defence against them. As a result it might be just possible that our excellent air division in Europe might find itself helpless to cope with an attack from the east, if it turned out to be an attack of that type.
Therefore, if one could justifiably go on that premise-I realize there are a lot of ifs -our air division could be used to better advantage on Canadian soil. So far as I know there are no V-2 types of rockets being developed which would be capable of reaching the large industrial centres of this continent from Asia or Europe, but it is highly probable that they will be developed in the next 5 or 6 years, and that is a possibility we should not lose sight of. It is vitally important, therefore, to have research into the development of rockets which could be used in a defensive way to intercept weapons of this type.
When one considers the horrible possibilities of an atomic war brought upon us by rockets-and it is not fantastic; it is quite within the realm of possibility-which we are incapable of intercepting or destroying in any way before they arrive, one is faced with a horrible vision. We must realize that our first responsibility, and it is a very great one, is to make sure that our defences are so 50433-382J
Supply-National Defence efficient that no would-be aggressor would dare attack. We can then hope that position will remain long enough to allow would-be aggressors to attain sanity. Even in the last two wars it could not be said that there was such a thing as winning the wars, because victory was attained at such a tremendous cost in life and treasure as to be practically indistinguishable from defeat. That would be even truer if a third world war should occur.
I do not want to end on such a dismal note, and I do not mean to imply that the world is hurtling toward inevitable selfdestruction. Nevertheless we should not assume that progress is inevitable. Change is inevitable; progress must be achieved. It behooves us to see that we make suitable progress, pre-eminent progress in the field of national defence, so we can deter aggressors until a better age dawns.
It has been said that the only hope of deterring aggression is to be in a position to retaliate, and I think that is true. Field Marshal Montgomery had something to say in that regard and I quote:
We stand today at the crossroads not knowing which turning to take. Absolute defence against ail- attack will be impossible in the future. A deterrent, the means with which to hit back instantly and to give more than you receive, is the surest way to make an aggressor think twice before he attacks. The west must build up such a deterrent, capable of being delivered immediately through the air. It is then vitally necessary to guard against a surprise attack, and against treachery, and to be able to hold such an attack long enough to enable nations to spring to arms behind the shield and mobilize their collective strength.
That is almost a truism. That leads me to the possibility of the reassessment of Canada's role as far as the air force is concerned. As I have said, we have concerned ourselves almost entirely with defensive aircraft. I realize that a strategic air force would be a terrifically expensive undertaking, and I am not suggesting that Canada should think of building up such a force, as I think that would be beyond our capabilities and capacities. We can speak only for ourselves in this regard, but I think consideration should be given to supporting what might be termed a British commonwealth strategical air force.
As I have said, such a force is the only means of immediate retaliation which we would have at our disposal. At the present time we are depending almost entirely on the strength of the United States in that regard. I should like to see renewed consideration given to the possibility of Canada supporting one squadron of a strategic air force which would be a combined effort of the whole British commonwealth. The last war demonstrated that the commonwealth can co-operate magnificently in efforts of that

Supply-National Defence type. The day may come when we will regret not having made any contribution toward a strategic air force of that type. Of course the development of suitable aircraft would have to be left to some larger country, either the United Kingdom or the United States. Equipment of United States design could be used, or perhaps some of the new V-class bombers which are coming into use in the United Kingdom.
While on this subject of equipment I should like to refer briefly to the whole policy of reequipping our air force when the present equipment becomes obsolete or obsolescent. I think we should make our contribution in the design field, so we would not get into the position of having only one egg and therefore incapable of having it in more than one basket. I think we are in a weak position when we have to depend entirely on the success of one aircraft which is designed in Canada.
I should like to see some co-operative system devised in this field so the various governments could put out design contracts. Perhaps you would have a dozen attempts at one design requirement, and the most successful could be brought into production in all the countries under licence. I recognize that we are manufacturing aircraft under licence now, the most obvious example being the Sabre. But we should not overlook the fact that the United States is also manufacturing British aircraft under licence, as well as engines. Therefore I feel that we should look carefully at the wide field of aircraft design and be ready to manufacture for ourselves and perhaps the NATO nations aircraft designed by some other country, if they are superior to what we have designed ourselves.
At the present time there is a necessity for such a program, arising no doubt from the need of a suitable replacement for the Sabre. There was a news item in the papers yesterday referring to a new MIG design which was to be seen in Moscow. This could go much faster and was apparently superior to the Sabre equipped with the Orenda engine. Therefore consideration should be given to the manufacture of some later type of fighter aircraft under licence in this [DOT] country. The one that comes to mind is an aircraft which was designed for the United States navy. This is a fighter of exceptional performance known as the Chance Vought XF8U, I think it is. I just cite it as one example; no doubt there are other designs which might be considered as successors to the Sabre.
Having said that, I conclude my remarks by saying once again that if our defence efforts should in the end prove to be unsuccessful it will probably be due to the fact that we have developed a sort of Maginot line complex, the idea that we here on the North American continent can protect ourselves against attack. With modern developments I do not think that is the case, and collectively we must be ready to deter aggression by having the means of rapid and powerful retaliation.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
